item.title: The Wilderness Diaries, Episode 5: The Real World
item.description:
The day has come. It feels like an interview and, believe it or not, I am stressed. This is new, something I never thought I would do. The shame, at least, has gone.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
I am here for a reason. I keep hearing that the job market is buoyant, and that youth unemployment is a disaster, which is true. But I rarely hear about the over-50s, whose situation I think is just as serious. That is why I wanted to claim Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA): so that my age group is counted and the problem becomes visible in the official figures. The money? It matters, but at £95.55 a week, with children in education, it is a drop in the ocean. I would encourage anyone in my position to claim.
I treat the appointment as an interview, because the officer can still refuse my application.
I dress like the old days: business casual, pointy shoes. No flashy watch, no flashy phone, no flashy bike on display. This is modern London, after all, and I would rather not get mugged. I park my old bike outside, next to a striped one. Not reassuring.
I walk to the entrance with my helmet on and am startled to find two security guards by the doors. They politely ask me to leave the helmet at the entrance. Why? This is ridiculous. I would understand why at my second appointment.
I am asked whom I am meeting and sent down an interminable walkway. Civil servants are busy with claimants on every side. Some claimants look agitated, even desperate; most look calm, almost empty-minded. Halfway along, another security guard. I get weird looks, probably because of what I am wearing. Upstairs, yet another guard asks me to wait.
As I remember it, the officer checks my credentials and asks about my old job, what I do all day, what I am applying for. “I expect you to look for work all day long,” he says. Really? I did not know that. I fire up my laptop and show him the companies I have applied to. He is not impressed, merely indifferent. My 150 lines of Excel are a blur to him. “You need to stay in the country,” he adds, and I half expect him to ask for my passport.
I ask whether he has met many finance people lately. Not a huge change, he says, which I find bizarre. He would revise that assessment a fortnight later.
Quietly, because other claimants are nearby, I tell him about my mental struggle. I feel useless, unloved, incapable. He says he understands and that I need to keep going. For someone of my calibre, he reckons, it will take six to nine months to find something. I know that already. It does not make me feel any better.
He asks whether I use the professional social network and checks my profile. He offers help with my CV. Then, in a funny kind of way, he advises me to apply to a specific company. I ask him to look at its careers page, which I have already checked. “Nothing suitable for you,” he adds. I know.
Fifteen minutes later, he is keen to move on and books another meeting for two weeks’ time. I leave, head down, mind down, humbled. I collect my helmet. My bike is still there, wheels attached.
I ride home, fire up the laptop, £95.55 richer than an hour ago, and start looking for new roles. Because clearly I was not doing that before

The Wilderness Diaries, Episode 3: The Social Misfits </news/losing-your-job-in-banking-3>
The Wilderness Diaries, Episode 2: Cutting the Cloth </news/losing-your-job-in-banking-2>

item.title: Hedge fund Taula Capital doubled pay to £959k per head last year (on average)
item.description:
Many hedge funds are having a bad year, but some are having a terrible year and Diego Megia's Taula Capital Management </news/diego-megia-taula-capital>is among them.
Taula's performance for October hasn't been disclosed, but in late September the fund was down over 9%. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-24/hedge-fund-taula-down-9-4-in-volatile-year-for-macro-traders>Markets have not been kind in the intervening weeks.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
It was not always thus. Taula Capital Holdings Ltd. just released accounts for the year ending December 2025, and in that year the nascent fund generated £92.3m in revenues and £4.8m in profits, up 152% and 40% respectively on the previous period on an annualised basis.
As revenues and profits rose, Taula Capital Holdings increased its average total headcount by 19 to 73 people. It almost doubled average compensation to £959k. And it spent £1.2m on recruitment and development.
Taula Capital has multiple UK entities, including Taula Capital Holdings Ltd, Taula Capital Management (UK) LLP and Taula Capital Limited.
Taula Capital Management was launched in 2023 and officially began trading in mid-2024. It pursues a discretionary global macro strategy and many of its people, including Megia and deputy CIO Stefan Ericsson </news/london-s-top-new-hedge-fund-has-millennium-s-alleged-50m-man>are ex-Millennium.
Taula didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-31/diego-megia-s-hedge-fund-taula-raises-1-75-billion-in-new-cash> reported in March that Taula had $8.5bn in assets under management after raising $1.75bn from investors. Previous reports <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-06-03/ex-millennium-trader-megia-debuts-own-hedge-fund-with-5-billion> suggested that $3bn of the $5bn launch capital came from Millennium.
This week Millennium reportedly withdrew $1.5bn <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-02/millennium-pulls-over-1-5-billion-from-two-external-hedge-funds>from two external hedge funds - Troluce Capital Advisors and Axebrook capital - that lost money.
Taula declined to comment on its performance.

item.title: Who deserves the biggest bonuses after 2026? Probably not you
item.description:
2026 still has a few weeks to go, but there are some things clearly shaping up. Revenues are up pretty comfortably </news/bofa-q3-2026> across the board. Banks are cutting headcount </news/barclays-ai-job-cuts>, mostly due to AI. Those two things should have a pretty clear conclusion: less people and more money means bigger bonuses.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Reality is more complex. Data from market intelligence provider Tricumen suggests that some groups of people did very well – but many were simply flat. Mostly.
The best performing product groups, and by implication the ones who can expect the biggest bonuses at the end of the year, are people who work in equities sales & trading </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank>. Tricumen found that the average front-office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> professional working in equities generated $4.2m in operating revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up by 31% on the $3.2m they had generated on average in the same period of 2025.
Equities professionals were strong all around (all were generating substantially more revenue) but by far the biggest increases came from those in prime services – those who work with hedge funds. Prime services professionals earned 38% more revenue per head in the first nine months of 2026 than they did in the same period of 2025, and this was a significant increase on how much they earned in 2024, too.
Also doing well were some bankers. Debt capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> (DCM) bankers were mostly flat from a revenue-generating point of view, but their siblings in equity capital markets (ECM) and M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> were doing well – the former 38% up YoY, and the latter 25% up YoY.
Broadly speaking, professionals in fixed income, currencies, and commodities (FICC) were doing worst. Currency and rates traders were flat on 2025, and credit traders barely above. Only commodities traders were up substantially (by around 9%), but given the strong performance of the sector – and how in demand they are </news/commodities-trading-hiring> with employers – it’s rather disappointing.
Forecasting the rest of the year is, of course, difficult. The overwhelming success of the Democratic party in the midterms – and their open hostility towards AI-related investment <https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/democrats-planning-flood-ai-bills-when-they-take-control-congress-2026-11-06/> – will likely crimp bankers, at the very least, who had hundreds of billions in deals lined up.

item.title: Barclays' 27-year-old new whale trader has made a huge splash
item.description:
As we have reported, Barclays has several new rates traders in London and they have interesting if unofficial names.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
There is Mark the Whale Wade </news/barclays-hired-the-whale-from-nomura>, aged only 27 who just joined from Nomura. There is Italian stallion Julian Ercole </news/julien-ercole-barclays>who just joined after an outing to hedge fund Point72. There is Graham Bates from Capula and JPMorgan, who is also known as G-Unit </news/graham-bates> and whose arrival is thought to have sparked a run of G-Unit trainer <https://www.reebok.eu/en-gb/products/g-unit-g6-mens-trainers-100289469-289469?variant=58630713770332>purchases for Barclays to send to clients; they are now sold out.
So far, though, it's Wade who appears to be having the best week. Barclays declined to comment for this article and Wade didn't respond to a request to comment, but multiple sources say Wade had a huge day yesterday even if hedge funds didn't. </news/hedge-fund-manager-unemployed>
The extent of the hugeness is not known but we understand that it was related to the Bank of England's decision to increase the interest rate to 4%. Wade called it right and is thought to have had a "monster" day.
This is good news for Barclays, whose European rates traders underperformed in the third quarter and which recently lost head of European rates Hamza Hoummady. </news/barclays-s-head-of-european-rates-trading-is-leaving>
The only fly in this ointment may be competition between Barclays' three new big beasts. In a move that is thought to have annoyed its rates traders, Barclays reportedly <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-22/barclays-prime-and-derivatives-traders-drive-equities-windfall> redirected capital to its Asia prime broking business in the third quarter. The three new macro traders, are understood to be competing for the remaining pool. Ercole and rates sales star Puni Rajah </news/punitha-raja-barclays> are thought to be making their own ripples, but it's the 27-year-old whale that is currently causing the biggest displacement of water there.

item.title: From $15m sign-on bonuses to unemployment. The hedge fund lives of late 2026
item.description:
As has been frequently expressed, it's a bad time for hedge funds. </news/hedge-fund-meltdown>Bloomberg <https://x.com/nishantkumar07/status/2118413906469343576> has a chart showing performance by fund for the year to October. It suggests that many funds are already below Ken Griffin's performance hurdle for a viable hedge fund, of the risk free rate plus 4%. Based on the current three month treasury yield, this rate is now over 8%.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
November may be worse again. Funds were already dismissing portfolio managers </news/as-hedge-fund-walleye-capital-ejects-p-ms-a-reminder-of-the-toxic-interview> (PMs) closing pods and returning cash. The market - already saturated with unwanted macro and credit portfolio managers - is now saturated with some more.
"There will be a big wash," says one experienced portfolio manager and former Goldman MD, referring to a cleaning out of hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> talent. "It is not an easy life," he reflects.
Mike Alfaro, CIO of Gallo Partners, a New York-based long short equity fund, says 108 pods have been closed and that he's been bombarded with calls. "Headhunters I've never spoken to before were calling me one after another, asking if we were hiring yesterday. Someone called from Engineer's Gate," he says. "We've received a lot of resumes."
Last month, we reported that 100 people were out </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up> of London hedge funds alone in the macro space. Since then, departures have gone parabolic. It's been a sharp, swift turnaround, says Alfaro citing one portfolio manager in his early 40s whose fortunes have suddenly changed. "Earlier this year he was up 14% with a supposedly fully hedged market neutral book and now he is down 9% and has been fired," he says. That same portfolio manager had been receiving offers from major multistrategy funds dangling $15m sign-on bonuses. He'd been holding out for more and for a $6m year-end bonus where he was. Now he's unemployed.
Many of those being let go only recently joined. Anil Gondi </news/as-hedge-fund-walleye-capital-ejects-p-ms-a-reminder-of-the-toxic-interview>, who was running Walleye's equity long short business, only joined in 2025, following a year of gardening leave after departing from Balyasny in June 2024. Engineers Gate reportedly <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/engineers-gate-parts-ways-with-most-of-synthesis-stock-team?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>cut its 'stock synthesis team', including Mike Daylamani, who joined in only January 2025. Brevan Howard cut David Heinau, who joined in only December 2025. Heinau previously spent eight happy years as the head of proprietary trading at TD Securities in London.
What now? Hedge fund jobs have never been sure things. Daylamani at least has been cut before - in 2019 his team was reportedly <https://www.businessinsider.com/balyasny-cut-a-10-person-team-many-who-joined-less-than-two-years-ago-2019-8> despatched by Balyasny too. Daylamani bounced back from that, moving first to Schonfeld and then to Engineers Gate, where he ran his strategy based on "a hybrid human plus machine structure that separates idea generation (human) from idea monetization (machine)" and advised analysts to become "research architects" and go "AI native." He may yet return to say this somewhere else.
The most pain is being felt at the bottom of the hedge fund hierarchy, among junior traders who only joined funds in the past few months. One told us he's having a "tough time" and that the buyside is being "squashed." - "It was hard enough going from the sellside to a fund but now you have this rate move and the wars and it's too much to handle," he said.
It's not yet clear how portfolio managers' pain will percolate through to the broader hiring market, or to bonuses for salespeople and traders in banks. Equities desks in banks had been having an exceptional year, with revenues per head up over 30% according to market intelligence provider Tricumen. They will be expecting big bonuses, but if the market is awash with hedge fund talent, the pressure to pay will be less.
Much depends upon what happens next in the market, says Alfaro. "If there is a V-shaped recovery, you will see a V-shaped recovery in momentum demand," he says. "I do not think there will be a V-shaped recovery," he adds.
If the recovery does not come, Alfaro predicts there will be a reconsideration of what portfolio management involves. In bond markets, credit PMs have been accused of being "morons" </news/hedge-funds-hired-too-many-morons-and-other-unpopular-opinions-as-the-industry-pukes-p-ms> and simply going long bonds. In macro, they've been accused of </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up> "just using EGBs as a carry asset. Buying bonds, sitting on the carry and getting a percentage cut." In equities, Alfaro says PMs that sold themselves as market neutral were really just trading market pops. "That’s why so many guys will get fired," he says. "They all do the same thing – they have a thesis but the moment the market moves against them they have no confidence in their investing ability and chase momentum." His own fund is up slightly in November and is "flattish" on the year. There will be more emphasis on finding really good risk-takers, says Alfaro. "There are a few good people out there and that is really going to become known now."
The clear out may create opportunities for a new generation of traders. It may also suppress hiring and pay. "I can't imagine this will be a good year for anyone," says one veteran credit trader. "Hedge funds now have a larger talent pool to choose from, but I'm not sure many will be out hiring."
There could be beneficiaries of the rout. The junior trader who recently moved to a fund says he wishes he'd joined Jane Street </news/how-to-get-a-job-at-jane-street>or Citadel Securities instead. "I would have been better off there," he reflects.

item.title: Who exactly are Goldman Sachs' 109 new partners?
item.description:
As of today, Goldman Sachs has some new partners. 109 of them, to be exact, an absolutely huge class - the biggest class since 2010, way up on the 95 it promoted in 2024 </news/goldman-sachs-partners-list-2024>, and way way up on the 80 it promoted in 2022 </news/2022/11/goldman-sachs-partners-2022>.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Goldman Sachs’ partners are a by-product of when the firm was legally a partnership (it went public as a corporation in 1999), but there are very, very real perks attached. A salary of more than $1m, for example. A share of a special bonus pool. And the opportunity to invest in Goldman's own funds, which provide carried-interest </news/what-is-carried-interest> style compensation. A lot of money. Plus David Solomon or John Waldron call you to tell you, which is fun.
62 of the firm's new partners are in the Americas, 27 are in EMEA, and 20 are in Asia. Around 40% of them joined the firm from university - lifers - and around 60% joined from a rival firm. The youngest, by our estimations, are around 34, and the oldest are in their mid-50s.
The most represented cities - in order - were New York (47 partners), London (22), and Hong Kong (9). India had just 2 employees named partner, fewer than Japan's 3, despite Goldman having 8,000 people in India, and around 1,000 in Japan.
But - without further ado - here is the Goldman Sachs Partner Class of 2026:
Vikas Agrawal - MD, Co-Head of Energy Transition and Climate, Private Credit Also ran the bank's Alternative Energy Investing group for 17 years from 2006.
Raul Aldrey - MD, Global Head of Marcus Engineering The least-tenured (at Goldman) person on the list. Came from Citi in only June 2025, so made partner after 17 months at the firm.
Felicity Anderson - MD, XVA Trading head An Oxford physicist who joined straight from university in 2013. At about 35, she's one of the youngest partners in the class.
Craig Balenzuela - MD, Head of Australia & New Zealand Client Business, Asset Management A late arrival from Australian state-backed fund manager QIC in 2022. Made partner within five years of walking through the door. Not bad.
Guillaume Banderet - MD, Inflation Trading An inflation trading specialist who did stints at UBS and Deutsche. Partner just 13 years after leaving university, making him one of the youngest on the list.
Joshua Banschick - MD, Mortgage Trading Survived Bear Stearns' 2008 collapse, rode the rescue into JPMorgan, and has now made partner trading mortgages. Ironic? Maybe a bit.
Sushil Bathija - MD, Head of M&A and Consumer Retail Group, Asia ex-Japan Has been an MD since 2016. Patience does get rewarded.
Christian Beerli - MD Arrived as a Zurich academic, working as a finance research and teaching assistant, and has been at Goldman for 20 years. In Hong Kong, obviously.
Dennis Beeson - MD, Private Bank Former EY accountant who has spent 20 years at Goldman, moving from distressed debt to asset finance to the private bank.
Alexander Blostein - MD, Equity Research (Financials) Research partners are rare. He covers asset managers, brokers, and exchanges, among others.
David Bodenstein - MD, Head of European IG, Levfin and Macro Trading
Erin Briggs - MD, Equity Derivatives Sales
Pierre Brunet - MD, Co-Head of EMEA Commodity Sales Joined Goldman in 2008. Seen a lot since then.
Thomas Campbell - MD, Equity Derivatives and Convertible Bond Sales A Boston lifer. Went from Boston College straight into Goldman's Boston office 23 years ago. Boston, Boston, Boston. Might be a New York Yankees fan.
Yufeng Cao - Head of Asia Commodities Trading; Co-Head of Global Oil and Products Trading Runs one of Goldman's most profitable trading businesses.
Daphne Chan - MD, CEO, Goldman Sachs Asset Management Singapore Joined in 2010 selling money market funds, and now runs GSAM in Singapore.
Lily Chan - MD, Alternative Investments At Credit Suisse before joining Goldman in 2012.
John Chappell - MD, Engineering An elder statesman, really: joined Goldman Sachs International in 1997, nigh on 30 years ago, but was only made MD in 2020.
Omar Chaudhary - MD, Head of Alternatives Multi-Strategy Solutions, Americas A 26-year veteran who raised money for Goldman's private credit push before swapping Manhattan for Newport Beach, California. Can you blame him?
Sung Cho - MD, Co-Head of US Fundamental Equity and Public Tech Investing Could have been a concert pianist, as he spent nine years in Juilliard's pre-college programme before becoming a stock picker.

Anupam Damani - MD, Co-Head of Global Emerging Markets Debt A star hire from Nuveen in 2023 and a former Bond Manager of the Year. Made partner within three years of arriving. Not bad at all.
Adam Dawson - MD, Global Co-Head of Healthcare Private Equity A Canadian chemical engineer turned healthcare investor.
Rohan Deshpande - MD and Technology Fellow, Head of Application Development Platform Joined from Amazon Web Services, where he was a principal engineer and founding member of the GraphQL Foundation's board.
Zachary Eckler - MD
Gaudenz Eichenberger - MD
Chris Emmerson - MD Jumped ship from Merrill Lynch in 2009, a year after Bank of America's rescue takeover. Has spent 17 years at Goldman since.
Andrew Fisher - MD, Global Head of Asset Liability Management Spent twenty years trading derivatives before this. Goldman lifer of 21+ years.
Francesca Gardner - MD, Global COO, Human Capital Management and Corporate Workplace Solutions Started her career in press relations, of all things, at Brunswick.
Akhil Garg - MD, Structured Finance
Luke Gordon - MD, Head of M&A for Global Industrials 27-year veteran of Goldman. Patient, we presume.
Simon Gosling - MD Joined from Deutsche in 2008 and spent 11 years as an MD before making partner.
Brian Greeff - MD, Global head of Prime Services Operations, Client Onboarding Operations, and Fees and Commissions Operations One of the older new partners, having graduated in 1997. Former board chair of the Utah Opera.
Brian Grzelakowski - Midwest Region Head, Private Wealth Management A former college football player for the University of Illinois who now runs Goldman's wealth business across the Midwest. 5”11 and 215 pounds.
Anushka Gupta - MD, Head of Goldman Sachs Apex (Americas) Started as an analyst in July 2008, weeks before Lehman collapsed. Now runs Goldman's coverage of family offices across the Americas. Much safer job.
Puneet Gupta - MD, Head of Macro Synthetics Trading EMEA
Lalit Gurnani - MD, Investment Banking (TMT) A neuroscience graduate who worked in Lloyd Blankfein's Office of the Chairman early in his career. Now a tech banker.
George Horton - MD, Head of EMEA Business Services Investment Banking A Masters in Finance graduate from London Business School before joining Goldman as an associate. Partner within 15 years. Not bad.
Jehan Ilahi - Global Head of Investor Relations A former JPMorgan banker to financial institutions. Now sells Goldman to its own shareholders.
Karen Ip - MD, Senior Counsel A rare lawyer partner. Spent 20 years advising Goldman's Hong Kong business.
Yu Itoki - Japan Head of Private Equity and Growth Equity Joined straight out of the University of Tokyo in 2011 and now runs Japanese private equity investing in his late 30s. One of the younger partners on the list.
David Jeria - MD, Equity Execution A double MIT engineering graduate who spent a decade as a VP. Partner eight years after finally making MD.
Benjamin Johnson - MD, Global Head of Corporate Credit, Asset Management Probably the oldest of the new partners, at around 57.
Yugandhar Karna - MD Goldman lifer of 21 years.
Aron Kershner - MD, Co-Head of Portfolio Management, Quantitative Equity Solutions Spent nine years volunteering as a running guide for disabled marathon runners with Achilles International. Goldman lifer of more than two decades.
Banu Kisakurek - MD, Global Co-Head of Asset-Backed Finance A physicist who spent seven years in Istanbul doing deals for Goldman across Turkey and the Middle East. Now runs one of private credit's more exciting areas.
Michael Klym - CEO, Goldman Sachs Canada Practised as a lawyer at Calgary firm Bennett Jones before switching to banking. Now runs Goldman’s whole Canadian business. Not bad.
Kyle Kniffen - MD, Global Head of Alternatives, Third Party Wealth Came from BofA Merrill Lynch to sell Goldman's private funds to wealthy investors.
Praveen Korapaty - Chief Interest Rates Strategist A Wharton PhD who started at Lehman in 2005 and worked there through its collapse. Now Goldman's headline voice on interest rates.
Tibor Kossa - Co-Head of Investment Banking, Germany & Austria Spent 16 years at Credit Suisse before switching in 2018. Now co-runs Goldman's German banking business.
Kristin Kramer - MD, Global Head of Capital Introduction A Columbia history graduate who joined Goldman straight from college. On the younger side of the list -late 30s, by our calculations.
David Landers - MD, Healthcare Investment Banking Learned the business in Goldman's Executive Office and working directly for the head of investment banking. A healthcare banker and partner in his mid-30s.
Phillip Lee - MD, Head of Real Money Franchise, Global Interest Rate Sales

Nikhil Reddy - MD, Head of Real Estate, Asia Pacific, Goldman Sachs Alternatives Joined Goldman's Special Situations Group three months before Lehman failed. Now runs Asian real estate investing from Hong Kong. Career timing has appeared to improve dramatically.
Mark Romanczuk - Americas Commercial Real Estate Lending Named one of the most powerful players in commercial real estate finance by Commercial Observer <https://commercialobserver.com/power-series/player/mark-romanczuk-siddharth-shrivastava-timothy-richards-and-andrew-white/>.
Neil Rudisill - MD, Investment Banking Studied “Global Governance and Diplomacy” at Oxford. Also a former consultant. Joined Goldman as a VP from Barclays around a decade ago.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Market thugs attack hedge fund jobs while Goldman Sachs phones explode. Weird omission from the Goldman partner list
item.description:
Yesterday was a day for metaphor. Taking a cold bath didn't quite describe it. Hedge fund coach Denise Shull told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-06/crowded-hedge-fund-trades-are-unwinding-fast-after-ugly-october?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261106&utm_campaign=author_19458291> it was more like "being attacked in a parking lot by three thugs.” - “Your instinct is to fight back, and in some ways you have to — just long enough to find an opening to run.” John Flood, head of Americas execution services at Goldman Sachs, said phones had been "exploding."
This wasn't literally so. Clients were calling with requests for "colour", said Flood. Goldman wasn't giving it but the more prosaic version of events was that hedge fund pods were blowing up amidst a sell-off of stocks related to the AI and data centre boom. Hedge fund bets have become highly leveraged. Last month the FT <https://www.ft.com/content/d313d0ce-d552-463e-9e84-6fa8c3efeeec?syn-25a6b1a6=1>reported that when derivative exposures are taken into account, the biggest hedge funds are 15-20 times levered. Yesterday, that started to show as crowded and highly correlated bets unwound.
After a brutal October in which many funds (Citadel excepted </news/people-analytics-hedge-funds>) lost money <https://x.com/nishantkumar07/status/2118413906469343576>, we may be on track for an even more thuggish November. Funds are dumping staff. Walleye cut a large portion </news/as-hedge-fund-walleye-capital-ejects-p-ms-a-reminder-of-the-toxic-interview> of its long short equities team. Engineers Gate cut <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/engineers-gate-parts-ways-with-most-of-synthesis-stock-team?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter> most of its 'stock synthesis team' which worked on a combination of discretionary and systematic trades. Brevan Howard cut some more credit traders. <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/five-credit-portfolio-managers-leave-hedge-fund-brevan-howard>There are unconfirmed suggestions of further cuts at other big funds. Almost certainly, more portfolio managers will be out.
The meltdown comes at an unfortunate time for market pundits like Scott Rubner at Citadel Securities, who declared on Wednesday <https://www.citadelsecurities.com/news-and-insights/global-market-intelligence/november-the-setup-improves/> that the buyers were "coming back" and there was "considerable capacity for investors to rebuild risk," or David Solomon </news/david-solomon-goldman-sachs>, CEO of Goldman Sachs, who said on Tuesday <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2026-11-03/goldman-s-solomon-sees-very-robust-demand-for-ai-deals-video> that there was "very robust" demand for AI deals, even if some bets might fail.
Yesterday is leading some to question <https://www.reuters.com/world/ai-backlash-could-threaten-anthropic-ipo-timing-potential-investors-say-2026-11-05/>whether the much-anticipated Anthropic IPO will be shunted into the future, which would be bad news for all the Goldman Sachs bankers hoping to make big money in fees. </news/pay-business-development-hedge-funds>
There are significant risks ahead. Bruno Schneller, managing partner at a family office in Zurich, expressed them to Bloomberg: "As losses mount, risk managers may force funds to cut exposure, potentially triggering another wave of selling regardless of fundamentals.” No metaphors needed there.
Separately, the Goldman Sachs partner list <https://www.goldmansachs.com/pressroom/press-releases/2026/gs-partner-class-2026> is out and it is big and strange.
There are 109 people on the list, which is more than the 95 people made partners by Goldman in 2024 and the biggest class since 2010. The Financial Times <https://www.ft.com/content/2f7eadc8-e01e-45df-8fcc-275e3e100558?syn-25a6b1a6=1>notes that the new partners include 13 engineers. New APAC partners have more than doubled from eight to 20. New Paris partners have shrivelled from five to three.
If you're a Goldman Sachs MD and you didn't make partner in the huge promotion class, you might be sad. Also sad might be female and ethnic minority MDs who are no longer a source of boasting in partner promotions. The New York Post <https://nypost.com/2026/11/05/business/goldman-sachs-buries-dei-metrics-as-it-names-biggest-partner-class-since-2010/> notes that Goldman buried its DEI metrics, which is weird given that the world has been flooded with memes about their return.
Meanwhile...
Ex-JPMorgan chief market strategist, Marko Kolanovic: </news/marko-kolanovic-jpmorgan> "With the end of Trump era, comes the end of AI/data center grift. Which was a scheme to create wealth for few, and illusion of prosperity for many (via stock market). And to give cover to otherwise reckless policies of wars, inflation, pollution and corruption." (X) <https://x.com/markoinny/status/2118374755086798999>
"There was massive derisking into midterms and traders were surprised by yesterday’s move and got sucked back in. HFs selling back pockets of the market (hyperscalers) that they bought yesterday. We are not seeing buyers step in to defend anything just yet." (X) <https://x.com/negligible_cap/status/2118389843210182896>
ING is dumping $500m of data centre loans. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/mystery-seller-puts-up-500-million-data-center-loans-backing-stargate-cyrusone>
Hedge fund VARA, which was big on AI, fell 33% in October. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/hedge-fund-vara-plunges-33-in-brutal-october-for-ai-stocks>
Paul Yablon is returning cash to investors from hedge fund Room30. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/ex-moore-money-manager-to-return-cash-from-his-hedge-fund?srnd=undefined>
Samlyn Capital is dismissing analysts and refocusing on financial stocks. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-06/hedge-fund-samlyn-dumps-all-stocks-but-financials-cuts-staff>
Hedge fund managers and other major investors collectively spent more than $330m on the US midterm elections. They mostly wanted low taxes, scant regulation and support for Israel. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/1338f6b6-81b1-478b-9807-5cfe1fc39113?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
New Goldman Sachs partners are selected through an intensive “cross-ruffing” process that this year involved more than a thousand interviews with candidates’ senior colleagues. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/2f7eadc8-e01e-45df-8fcc-275e3e100558?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
UBS has shed more than 5,500 jobs since January and cut its spending on outside consultants by more than $800m. (FT) <https://www.ft.com/content/b024d943-4b2f-4481-bbcb-ed551db2a8dd?syn-25a6b1a6=1>
Millennium hired Citi banker Pranav Haridasan to lead its operations in India. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-05/hedge-fund-millennium-taps-ex-citi-banker-to-lead-india-business?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261106&utm_campaign=author_19458291>
Follow me on X <https://x.com/MadameButcher>. Follow me on LinkedIn. <https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarahbutcherjournalist/>

item.title: As hedge fund Walleye Capital ejects PMs, a reminder of the "toxic" interview
item.description:
First it was a bad time for macro portfolio managers. Then it was a bad time for credit portfolio managers. Now the times have come for equities portfolio managers. Especially those at Walleye Capital, which has reportedly made a 5.9% loss in October.
Bloomberg <https://x.com/nishantkumar07/status/2118378593915121721?a=ELDpXX5lRrXOchVMtH8&s=20> reported today that Walleye is returning some of its $17bn of capital to investors. Quoting a letter to investors from Walleye CEO Will England, Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/walleye-capital-stock-picking-head-anil-gondi-exit-2026-11>says the firm has cut Anil Gondi, the head of its equity long short business, along with a substantial portion of its long short team.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Walleye didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Business Insider says the firm plans to continue trading stocks but that internal teams will now report to England himself. England reportedly wrote that: "Over the past few years, we invested considerable effort in improving the internal business, including bringing in new leadership. Those efforts did not produce the results we expected, and the opportunity cost and resources consumed have been too high relative to the return."
England, who is now aged approximately 41, joined Walleye as a quant in 2013 and transformed the firm - which was previously an options market maker - into a multistrategy hedge fund. In September 2023, when Walleye had only $5bn in AUM, England gave a frank interview to Colossus <https://colossus.com/episode/england-a-primer-on-multi-strategy-hedge-funds/> in which he said that portfolio management jobs can be "toxic." </news/2023/09/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund>
"The job of being a PM, whether you're quantitative or fundamental, is psychologically extremely toxic because you're going to be wrong basically just as much as you're going to be right. You're going to get kicked in the face a lot, and you're going to be someone who's the smartest person that they've known their entire life, and then they're just going to get beat up all the time."
Today is one such toxic day.
Promisingly, perhaps, England also told Colossus that he tries to be fair to portfolio managers during drawdowns. “If you’re in a tough spot, you want to have a fair conversation about it as opposed to just essentially being fired by some 23-year-old because in the spreadsheet, the cell goes from green to red,” he opined.
It's not clear whether England has had a lot of these conversations of late. Walleye refocused on equities sales and trading after cutting credit </news/hedge-fund-walleye-closed-its-credit-team-and-bank-of-america-benefitted> teams in 2025 and global macro teams <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2024-10-29/walleye-cuts-five-traders-including-global-macro-head-anuraj-dua> in 2024. It hired Tom D'Angelis, <https://www.walleyecapital.com/bio/tom-deangelis> the former head of equities business development at Citadel in 2023, and hired new equities portfolio managers, including 38-year-old Anil Gondi himself, who came from Balyasny in July 2025. Maybe DeAngelis needs to find some new people now?
"It's been a very unfortunate October for them," observes one former Walleye PM. "It's a shame they weren't more diversified."

item.title: Mizuho brought in a Deutsche Bank saleswoman and made her an MD
item.description:
What would you do to become a managing director (MD) </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> in an investment bank? Most people would wait a long time to achieve it. It can take decades, after all. Some people, however, find a quicker way to do it: moving to a slightly smaller bank when you’re a director already.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Veronica Ames joined Mizuho yesterday in New York as an MD. She joined the firm from Deutsche Bank, where she spent 11 years in its risk management solutions team. The risk management solutions team, despite its name, is not a traditional risk management </news/risk-job-investment-bank> function. It is a sales team </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> that sells currency and commodities hedges, among others. Ames sold rates hedges.
Ames has had a wealth of experiences. She interned with Goldman Sachs’ private bankers and Barclays’ traders in the same year, before joining BMO Capital Markets’ derivatives sales team after graduation. Perhaps at Mizuho she will be in M&A </news/what-are-ma-jobs>, but probably not. Mizuho did not respond to a request to comment. In all likelihood, Ames will join Mizuho’s derivatives risk solutions team, which is analogous to what her team at Deutsche Bank did.
Deutsche Bank is certainly a bigger investment bank than Mizuho, but the move was probably a rather easy sell. A managing director role is highly coveted in finance, and Mizuho is a perfectly respectable place to achieve it. The downside? The firm also has “senior managing directors”, like many boutique banks </news/boutique-investment-banks> such as Evercore do. Another rung to climb.

item.title: Citi's new financial sponsors banker arrived, and an old one is looking for adventure
item.description:
As has been observed elsewhere today <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroups-former-head-of-financial-sponsors-khullar-to-exit-bank-3b5dc290>, Ashu Khullar is leaving Citi. Khullar wrote on his LinkedIn profile that he is retiring from Citi after 38 years and an "extraordinary journey," but that he is also "looking forward to the next adventure."
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Khullar was briefly co-head of Citi's global asset managers and financial sponsors business. He moved into this role to the surprise </news/anthony-diamandakis-citi> of some people internally in early-2025, despite having spent much of his career at Citi in corporate banking <https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/citi-set-to-name-top-apac-exec-as-india-ceo/articleshow/68324141.cms> and having previously run Citi's entire business in India <https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/citi-appoints-ashu-khullar-co-head-global-asset-managers-memo-shows-2025-02-05/> after a short period in APAC ECM.
Shortly after Khullar arrived, Anthony Diamandakis </news/anthony-diamandakis-citi>, Citi's star EMEA financial sponsors banker and Khullar's co-head, resigned and went to JPMorgan. So, too, did Keith Heller, another financial sponsors banker on the Citi team.
Khullar's own departure coincides with but may not be directly related to the arrival of Klaus Hessberger </news/klaus-hessberger-lazard-citi>, whom Citi hired from Lazard long ago in April. After a period of gardening leave, Hessberger wrote on LinkedIn two weeks ago that he had started "an exciting new chapter as co-head of Citigroup‘s global financial and strategic Investor Coverage Group."
The various changes in Citi's financial sponsors team have occurred during the times of Vis Raghavan <https://www.ft.com/content/6584b0fc-ea9e-4a0d-80ea-dde8b1063545?syn-25a6b1a6=1>, also from JPMorgan, who became head of Citi's investment bank in July 2024.
Hessberger and Raghavan previously worked together at JPMorgan and Raghavan has hired many other JPMorgan former colleagues too. At least 12 are now in key roles at Citi. </news/is-citi-preparing-for-another-hot-summer-of-jp-morgan-hires>
Citi's M&A business has grown by substantially less than US rivals </news/citi-m-and-a>this year. There are suggestions that clients are waiting to see how the new team beds in. With Khullar gone, they may need to wait a bit longer.
Citi didn't comment. Former colleagues of Khullar at Citi say he is a talented leader who quickly stepped up in the financial sponsors role and developed close client relationships during his brief tenure.

item.title: Citadel Securities hired someone to grow their cryptocurrency business, of all things
item.description:
Financial services as an industry has been investing heavily into AI. But the previous (technological) flavor of the day - cryptocurrency - has not faded away completely. In fact, some firms are now investing in their capabilities here - including electronic market making firm </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> Citadel Securities (CitSec).
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Willis Croft joined CitSec last month as the market maker’s head of business development for digital assets, based in London. He joined the firm from Wintermute, a crypto-specialized algorithmic trading firm based in London, where he was a director in its business development & partnerships team. Before that, Croft was a VP at Genesis, the cryptocurrency exchange, until it shut its doors in 2023.
The embracing of digital assets by CitSec is rather incredible, in the grand scheme of things. Just five years ago <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-10-04/griffin-sees-crypto-mania-as-jihadist-call-against-the-dollar>, the firm’s founder, Ken Griffin, called cryptocurrency a “jihadist’s call” against the dollar. “I wish all this passion and energy that went into crypto was directed toward making the United States stronger,” Griffin told Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-10-04/griffin-sees-crypto-mania-as-jihadist-call-against-the-dollar>. Citadel Securities did not respond to a request for comment.
The firm has rather changed its tune since its founder’s comments. At the start of 2025, it planned to become a liquidity provider to cryptocurrency exchanges including Coinbase and Binance, among others. Since then, it began offering liquidity to Kraken, at the very least, which it also invested $200m into in November last year <https://blog.kraken.com/news/800-million-raise-to-advance-strategic-roadmap>.
CitSec’s job listings include <https://www.citadelsecurities.com/careers/details/systematic-crypto-trader/> one for a systematic crypto trader, and it refers to its digital assets team as “fast-growing.” The listing asks for “deep familiarity with centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.” If only Mr. Griffin could see it now.

item.title: UBS's high yield trading team may be going through some more changes
item.description:
UBS has got a newish head of high yield in the form of Robert Laux, who was its old head of EMEA leveraged trading before he left for a stint at BofA. Laux returned to UBS after nearly four years away in March 2026 </news/ubs-s-new-head-of-high-yield-trading-is-leaving-now-that-it-has-an-even-newer-one> and now it seems that his team there may be making some moves.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
UBS declined to comment for this article, but it's thought that Shaun Barlow, who joined UBS in 2022 to run EMEA leveraged finance trading to replace Laux while Laux was at Bank of America, may be moving on. Barlow also declined to comment. He is still registered as working for the bank on the FCA Register.
Barlow began his career as an equity derivatives trader at Goldman Sachs before the financial crisis. Then he moved to credit trading at Goldman, jumped to JPMorgan and transmogrified into the head of high yield and distressed trading at Nomura.
Barlow left Nomura in 2018 when the Japanese bank pulled back from distressed trading. He surfaced at Seaport Global in late 2019 according to the FCA Register, and left again for UBS in October 2022.
Now Barlow may be moving on again.
UBS's credit trading business is run by Jonathan Fletcher in London. Barlow is thought to have been one of Fletcher's hires. Previous recruits include Bharat Gupta, another former head of European high yield trading at UBS who left after 15 months in June 2026, and Carlo Armillis who joined from NatWest in August 2023 and left in October 2024.
European high yield traders </news/european-high-yield> as a group are having a hard time. Some European credit hedge funds are having an even harder one. </news/arini-capital-office>

item.title: Boutique banks are hiring senior bankers, and Lazard might be paying them more cash than before
item.description:
Q3 reporting season is wrapping up for America’s boutique investment banks </news/boutique-investment-banks> (just Moelis left). Some have done great, like Evercore </news/evercore-q3-2026>, and some haven't, like PJT </news/pjt-q3-2026>. Regardless, there is one thing they mostly have in common. Hiring.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Boutique banks have been on a hiring warpath since the start of the year. “2026 is shaping up to likely be our biggest partner recruiting year ever,” said Paul J Taubman, CEO of PJT Partners, on the firm’s Q3 analyst call. Perella Weinberg Partners (PWP) has also added nearly three times as many partners in 2026 already as it did in 2025 overall. “We intend to continue adding talent,” said PWP CEO Andrew Bednar on the call.
PWP’s growth is rather substantially in part due to its acquisition of Gleacher Shacklock </news/pwp-cuts-tim-shacklock>, a London-based boutique bank, and is also obfuscating the fact that the firm cut around 10% of its staff, including 12 partners.
Still, not every firm grows with acquisitions. Evercore, for example: “We hire people one-by-one,” said CEO John Weinberg. “We are not looking for another deal to do." Evercore’s latest acquisition was also for a UK boutique: Robey Warshaw </news/evercore-s-new-robey-warshaw-employees-are-a-different-breed>.
The UK has been a standout region for boutiques, despite Europe's economic challenges. Lazard’s CEO, Peter Orszag, noted that its UK advisory business had both a record Q3 and record first nine months of the year. PWP and Evercore’s London acquisitions may have helped.
Lazard might be the exception. It is up just 10 dealmakers since the start of the year, while targeting 10-15 hires per year. That's less than PWP, and barely above what PJT hired, despite PJT having 57% fewer people than Lazard.
Lazard's new joiners might be paid more cash. The firm said it's considering a move to a less deferral-heavy model of compensation.
Lazard’s revolutionary new compensation structure is actually pretty common across its rivals. “The huge incentive here is to align this from an employee retention and attraction perspective,” said Tracy Farr, the firm’s CFO. “The real benefit is an improved quality of the ratio itself, a greater ability for management to manage the comp ratio within a particular year, and a more attractive compensation policy,” Farr said.
It's not happening yet, though. “We have not finally decided to do this,” Lazard CEO Peter Orszag said. “We will have more to say about that in the coming weeks and before year-end.” Unfortunately for Lazard’s bankers, they are accumulating even more deferred stock for the time being.

item.title: Morning Coffee: 36-year-old hedge fund manager's big new office comes at the wrong moment. Did Deutsche Bank waste $500m?
item.description:
Along with all the other stock picking factors like momentum, value, quality and the like, there’s a little used indicator which can sometimes be used to spot when previous outperformers might be about to take a turn for the worse. The “HQ Factor <https://www.wsj.com/articles/when-to-sell-look-at-the-hq-1491768486>” doesn’t stand for “high quality”; it’s a warning that when a company moves to a flashy new headquarters building, it’s time for investors to get out.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
There’s a certain amount of logic behind the rule. An expensive new building might be a sign of hubris, or of a company that is expanding too quickly and stretching its finances and capability. Chief executives have been known to get caught up in the pleasures of deciding on their new real estate and take their eye off the business. Alternatively, the fancy office rule can reflect mean reversion. Companies, and hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>, move into new premises to accommodate the growth that comes with success, but these extraordinary runs rarely last.
This final scenario fits the FT's <https://www.ft.com/content/29c178c1-2960-4670-b510-f90b4b559903?syn-25a6b1a6=1> description of the recent experiences of Hamza Lemssouguer </news/hamza-lemssouguer-arini> at Arini Capital <https://app.ft.com/content/29c178c1-2960-4670-b510-f90b4b559903?sectionid=home>. Lemssouguer has had a meteoric career ever since he generated 5% of Credit Suisse’s fixed income </news/2021/07/credit-suisse-top-traders-leaving> trading revenues on his own aged 29, </news/2020/01/deutsche-bank-bonus-cut> then left to found Arini. He's been through previous drawdowns </news/hamza-lemssouguer-arini-capital> in the high single digits to mid-teens of per cent, but has more normally generated returns between 10% and 25% per year. With the support of a large fan base among Gulf investors, it must have seemed like a reasonable move to take on no fewer than eight floors of space formerly occupied by Apollo, just around the corner from Hanover Square in Mayfair.
But just as luck wouldn’t have it, shortly after signing the lease, Arini got caught in a credit crunch, with several of its biggest positions (including the debt of Aston Martin </news/hamza-lemssouguer-arini-capital>, Merlin Entertainments and Very Group) going sour. This year, the total drawdown has reached 26%. And worse than that, the FT notes thatthe news is out on the Street, which means that other traders are shorting Lemssouguer’s holdings in the hope he’ll be forced to liquidate.
The HQ rule is by no means infallible, although we have to note that it did pick up signs of impending bad luck at Eisler Capital </news/hedge-fund-eisler-capital-s-fancy-new-offices-are-at-odds-with-cost-cutting-intentions> last year. Goldman Sachs, for example, has pretty much gone from strength to strength since moving into 200 West Street in November 2009. JPMorgan's new Park Avenue office </news/jpmorgan-office-park-avenue>went from costing $3bn to an estimated $6bn <https://www.wsj.com/finance/banking/jpmorgans-skyscraper-on-park-avenue-estimated-to-cost-around-6-billion-76881bb3>, and all seems to be fine. Lemssouguer is still in a position to raise new capital from investors; he had $1.5bn of commitments at the start of last month on re-opening a closed strategy. But it might raise an ironic smile at Arini Capital to realise that despite their modern and aggressive approach in the cutting edge markets for distressed credit and private investments, they’ve fallen to an age old proverb coined by a restructuring specialist <https://www.thetimes.com/travel/advice/bill-mackey-p0fnrcdqvpd> in the 1980s.
Elsewhere, ''
& </news/get-a-job-in-ma> </news/deutsche-bank-s-ex-citi-bankers> </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/citigroup-dealmaker-tweedie-joins-kbw-as-head-of-european-investment-banking-72366687?mod=topic_news> <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-04/ubs-cuts-about-200-london-jobs-as-credit-suisse-fusion-nears-end> <https://x.com/sequoia/status/2117961312143855764?s=20> <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-04/hudson-river-trading-joins-wall-street-s-prediction-market-shift?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261104&utm_campaign=author_19908303&leadSource=uverify%20wall> <https://www.ft.com/content/8e6d1ee5-daf5-462b-a213-4224e7afe232?syn-25a6b1a6=1> <https://www.businessinsider.com/learjet-crash-elites-reconsidering-private-air-travel-2026-11> <https://x.com/MadameButcher> <https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarahbutcherjournalist/> </about/editor-tips>

item.title: As Goldman Sachs restricts vibe coding, developers express how annoying it is
item.description:
If you're a salesperson or a trader who likes being busy on Github Copilot and you've designed some tools which you use to monitor trade flows, email content, or calculate prices, then you probably don't want to work for Goldman Sachs.
But maybe you don't want to work for any other banks either.
Bloomberg reported this week that Goldman restricted </news/ben-atlas>the use of vibe coding on Github and Claude Code to technical staff and strats. Traders who had been using the tools for things like 'monitoring client trading flows, modeling market changes and positions, and creating written and graphic content,' were peeved, said Bloomberg.
Goldman Sachs didn't comment for this article. One senior developer at the firm said there had been "massive pushback" about the restrictions, and that hundreds of tools have been developed by individuals in the period, with many of them improving personal productivity. "Vibe coding allowed senior and junior people to develop things according to their taste," he says. Goldman's salespeople and traders, "developed things which were pretty useful from people who had never coded before," he adds.
It's not clear what happens to those tools now. It's thought that Goldman's restriction on vibe coding came into place a few months ago and the firm isn't commenting on whether it's imposed a restriction on the use of tools previously created. Many have noted that Marco Argenti, Chief Information Officer of Goldman Sachs, said in July <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=grOykIdJPgs&t=1s> that the firm's business people, such as traders or private wealth staff, were creating non-productionised tools which were sent to engineers for "hardening."
It's this hardening that may have been the problem. A spokesperson for Goldman Sachs told Bloomberg, "“We make certain AI tools available to our people to determine the best use cases across different parts of the firm. After a period of experimentation where we assess a variety of factors including productivity and risk management, we put them in the hands of those who are best suited to leverage them for the long term.”
The senior developer at the firm suggests the sheer volume of tools being created is the issue. There was a "proliferation," he says. Data sensitivity was an issue. So was the fact that individual salespeople and traders had tools they owned themselves, that might be circulated to others on a team.
Goldman is far from the only bank experiencing this. A senior developer at JPMorgan said there's a similar problem there. "People outside tech vibe code whole UIs and products and then it's on engineering to explain why we can't just put it into production," he says.
The JPM developer says non-technical people simply transfer the load of work onto engineering. "They leave out the boring stuff like authentication, entitlements, end to end testing, build and deployment," he tells us. "You'll just get a load of slop that works locally for a demo."

item.title: Hedge fund Jain Global hired the ex-Credit Suisse guy who wanted $100m
item.description:
Hedge fund Jain Global is now managing money exclusively for Millennium </news/millennium-jain-global>but has hired a new person as head of SMA (separately managed account) investments in London. The person has an interesting back story.
Jain Global's new head of SMAs is Ryan Nelson, a former Credit Suisse employee who was in the public eye not so long ago.
Nelson is the ex-co-head of prime services at Credit Suisse. </news/2023/03/ryan-nelson-credit-suisse-ubs>He held the role between 2019 and 2021 and was running the business with John Dabbs when Archegos collapsed in 2021. Credit Suisse was Archegos' largest counterparty and the Swiss bank lost $5bn+, which contributed to its subsequent road to collapse. An independent report </news/2021/07/credit-suisse-staff-incompetent-archegos>subsequently commissioned by Credit Suisse said the prime services business had been mismanaged. It didn’t name individuals, but said neither of the business’s two co-heads had actively managed it or its risks.
Nelson and Dabbs were among nine people let go by Credit Suisse in 2021. The report said Credit Suisse had imposed financial penalties totalling around $70m, including, in some cases, cancelled deferred pay and clawbacks of past pay. It didn’t say who was penalised.
Dabbs is now working in bus dev </news/schonfeld-bus-dev> in Laguna Beach, California and has kept a low profile. Nelson, however, sought at least $7m in compensatory damages and at least $100m for reputational harm and lost future income from Credit Suisse in FINRA arbitration.
In March 2024 a FINRA panel awarded Nelson just over $590k. As part of those proceedings, it also recommended that the explanation of the reason for Nelson's termination from Credit Suisse submitted to the regulator should be: “Mr. Nelson was one of nine employees terminated, not for cause, in August 2021, after it became known that a business unit in which they held various executive positions sustained substantial financial losses.”
Nelson didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Jain Global didn't comment or elaborate upon what Nelson's new SMA role involves.
Nelson has had a hard time. In 2023, he wrote a since-deleted post on LinkedIn saying that, “From a professional perspective, I would never wish the past year on my worst enemy.” He said he had thrown himself into family life, which was tough. "It is far more exhausting than anything I have dealt with at work. Homework, mealtimes, after school clubs, sports practices, ballet, birthday parties, play dates, morning time, bedtime, bathing, clothing, homeschooling, waking up at night, sickness etc. It is really hard!"
Before joining Jain Global, Nelson's LinkedIn profile said that he spent three and a half years as head of portfolio construction for EMEA at Boothbay Fund Management. Nelson has not been registered with the FCA <https://register.fca.org.uk/s/individual?id=0034G00002k7c7uQAA>since he left Credit Suisse in 2021. It's not clear whether he will require registration in his new role.

item.title: Risk and compliance professionals in London can earn seven figures
item.description:
American banks pay their people very well. Everyone knows that. Over $2m in London </news/salaries-and-bonuses-goldman-sachs-jpmorgan-citi-baml-morgan-stanley> for senior bankers, on average – and it’s not just bankers. Because their middle office colleagues in audit </news/accounting-job-finance-banking>, risk </news/risk-job-investment-bank>, and compliance </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-compliance> can also earn some very, very big bucks.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
These professionals are usually categorised as providing “control functions”. Pillar III disclosures made by banks note the compensation of these professionals, although their definition is rather blurry. The European Banking Authority (EBA) describes them in a certain way, the UK uses an older definition (from 2017 rather than 2021), and banks can expand their definition. At a minimum, “control functions” should always be assumed to refer to audit, risk, and compliance professionals.
Either way, there is money to be made in these roles. The chart below shows average salaries and bonuses for the most senior control staff who are designated as material risk takers (MRTs) at US banks subsidiaries in London in 2025.
MRTs are defined as professionals whose “professional activities have a material impact on the risk profile of the firm,” and automatically include all people who earn more than £660k ($837k). While there are many bankers </news/the-investment-banking-recruitment-process> or traders </news/how-do-you-get-a-job-in-sales-and-trading-in-a-bank> who fit this criteria automatically, but not a lot of risk and compliance professionals.
As the chart shows, Goldman Sachs' senior London risk and compliance staff are paid by far the most, earning more than $1m on average in 2025, comprising an average salary of $495k and an average bonus of $567k. The worst paid are at Citi, where they earned average total compensation of $586k, comprising average salaries of $371k and average bonuses of $214k.
There was also a very interesting discrepancy in how many control functions MRTs each bank employed. Bank of America registered 62 in London in 2025, while Citi had just 7. That’s likely related to the flexibility in definitions that the EBA guidelines suggest.
Away from MRTs, pay for people in control functions was, understandably, not as generous. Figures above come from our 2026 Salary & Bonus Report </banking-compensation-guide>, which found that support functions – including operations – earned between $49k and $410k on average, depending on rank. Much of a support professional’s potential compensation growth came from their reaching VP and director ranks, when they more than doubled their previous earnings. It’s worth noting, however, that our data is worldwide and is not limited to just UK respondents.
Either way, control functions professionals earn much less than their front-office colleagues in investment banking or sales or trading do. Pillar III reports lump these all in together as “investment banking”, making a convenient front-office vs middle-office distinction.
For one, there are many more high-earning front-office professionals than control ones, even at Bank of America. They’re also paid much better, around twice as much on average, mostly owing to their ability to command larger bonuses.
It is important to note, however, that bonuses for control functions professionals are intentionally smaller than for front-office professionals. “The remuneration of employees engaged in control functions is determined independently from the businesses they support,” Barclays' 2025 Pillar III disclosure noted. “Remuneration for control function employees is less weighted towards variable remuneration compared to front-office employees.”

item.title: Citi’s global head of derivatives is going and it has a new one
item.description:
As we noted yesterday </news/citi-equities>, Citi's equities business has suffered some departures and might need some new hires. As we also noted yesterday, Citi's relatively poor third quarter in equities appeared to be the result of a miss in equity derivatives, which the bank said declined.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Against that backdrop, we understand that Citi is reshuffling its equities business and that David Haldane, its global head of derivatives and EMEA head of equities, is leaving. Haldane, who is thought to have stepped down a few weeks ago, is understood to have been replaced by Rob Smolen, Citi's London-based global head of exotics and hybrids trading.
Citi didn't comment on Haldane's exit. The reason for the changes is not clear.
Haldane joined Citi from JPMorgan in Australia in 2011 and transferred to London in 2014. He was reported to global head of equity derivatives trading in 2016 and reported to Fater Belbachir, who also worked for JPMorgan and who also has a derivatives background. Belbachir joined Citi in 2020.
Smolen also came to Citi via JPMorgan's equity derivatives team. He has been there since 2017. IFR <https://www.ifre.com/people-and-markets/2463737/moves-barclays-hires-smolen-for-senior-equities-trading-role>reported in the summer that Smolen was joining Barclays. Bloomberg notes that Citi gazumped him.
In a memo seen by eFinancialCareers, Fater Belbachir said Smolen will, "work alongside David and our regional leadership in Europe to ensure a smooth transition."
Citi's equity derivatives business was historically its strong point, given the combined experience of its senior team in London. Under Haldane, it hired various expensive people </news/2015/08/citi-is-still-building-out-its-equity-derivatives-function> including Nikhil Reddy, Anurag Jodhawa, Emmanuel Girod,and John Macpherson </2015/05/citigroup-has-poached-nomura-global-head-of-futures-and-options>to manage its growth.
Matthew Topping, a Citi futures and options sales trader also recently reappeared at Marex.

item.title: Point72 hired another Goldman Sachs partner as a technology executive
item.description:
As we've noted in the past, Point72 has a love for Goldman Sachs technologists </news/hedge-fund-point72-can-t-stop-hiring-goldman-sachs-tech-fellows> rivalled only, perhaps, by Citadel. Steve Cohen's hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> hired Goldman partner Ilya Gaysinskiy </news/point72-hired-a-goldman-sachs-partner-that-ran-tech-for-marcus-as-new-cto> to be its CTO in 2024 and has just hired another partner for another executive role.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Faisal Shamsee announced via LinkedIn that he is joining Point72 as its chief infrastructure engineering office, based in Singapore. He was most recently the firm's co-head of Singapore, and held several senior engineering roles including head of core engineering for Asia Pacific. Shamsee spent 25 years at Goldman, working as a systems administrator early in his career before rising to partner in 2022. We first reported on his departure from Goldman in April, </news/goldman-sachs-head-of-engineering-in-singapore-is-leaving-so-is-its-global-head-of-ficc-operations> at which point his next destination was unclear.
Goldman people are proliferating at Point72. Last year, it hired several of the bank's former 'tech fellows' (its most technically capable individuals), including Rahul Garde, </news/point72-hires-ex-goldman-sachs-md-and-technology-fellow-from-jp-morgan> Point72's head of platform infrastructure. Shamsee, however, appears to be the first Goldman partner to join the hedge fund since Gaysinskiy. Other notable Goldman alumni at the fund include Michael Fisher, an ex-strat </news/strats-jobs-investment-banks>MD who joined as chief risk officer in 2024. </news/point72-chief-risk-officer-michael-fisher-goldman-sachs>
Citadel </news/morning-coffee-what-it-s-like-when-citadel-really-wants-you-another-jp-morgan-expenses-case> was arguably the more popular destination for Goldman's top technologists in recent years. Ken Griffin's hedge fund hired Goldman CTO Umesh Subramanian </news/umesh-subramanian> to be its own CTO in 2018, then hired his replacement, Atte Lahtiranta, in 2024. Subramanian left Citadel earlier this year and his replacement, rather than another Goldmanite, was Amazon VP Matt Taddy, <https://www.pionline.com/people-on-the-move/pi-citadel-cto-matt-taddy-hedge-fund/> who joined last month.

item.title: Another array of traders appears to have left Nomura
item.description:
It was not so long ago that we were reporting regularly about traders leaving Nomura </news/nomura-paid-its-bonuses-and-now-some-traders-are-leaving>, and particularly leaving Nomura's macro business. At the time, there were complaints both of bonus disappointment and about the heavy hiring from ANZ. </news/nomura-keeps-hiring-singapore-macro-types-they-are-not-all-from-anz>Since, then things appeared to have calmed down a bit. Until now.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
In the past week, we understand that another five traders and one salesperson have left Nomura. Alongside Pawan Bhargava </news/one-of-nomura-s-top-singapore-prop-traders-resigned>, a veteran prop trader who left last week, we understand that the departures include: Ian Hildebrand, a G10 FX trader in the US; Sagar Sambrani, an FX options trader in the UK; Dimitri Desquiens, a rates trader in Singapore; Alastair Loe, an EM trader in Singapore; Timothy Doern, the head of futures and options sales trading in the US; and Fiona Tay a VP in equity sales.
Nomura declined to comment. Many of those contacted didn't respond to a request to comment and many are still listed as employed on local regulatory sites.
The apparent reasons for the exits are not clear. Some of those departing are understood to be taking time to decompress. Sambrani and others are understood to be enroute to new jobs.
Nomura’s second quarter results, released last week, showed equities revenues rising 19% year-on-year and fixed income revenues falling 2%. CFO Hiroyuki Moriuchi said rates revenue declined “amid rising rates globally” and that credit client activity “was subdued as spreads widened.” Wholesale had got off to “a somewhat slower start” in October, he added.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Hedge fund manager nearly blew up his firm, but knows how to keep a secret. The job interview that cost more than a billion dollars
item.description:
DE Shaw is famous for doing things a little bit differently compared to its competitors in the multistrategy hedge fund </news/big-multistrategy-hedge-funds> space. Although its funds have historically had something of a quantitative bias, DE Shaw doesn't just hire mathematicians and physicists; there are always a few spaces occupied by poets, philosophy graduates </news/2023/08/de-shaw-hedge-fund-hiring-painters-poets>and even Broadway actors. Not only that, but unlike most pod shops, losing 30% doesn’t necessarily get you fired – you can even end up being promoted to head of risk <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-11-03/how-hedge-fund-d-e-shaw-plans-to-stay-king-of-quant?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter&leadSource=uverify%20wall>.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Max Stone actually did that – he ran discretionary macro trading </news/2021/05/how-to-get-a-job-in-a-global-macro-fund>when the fund lost a huge amount in the 1998 Russian default <https://medium.com/@navnoorbawa/d-e-shaws-1998-crisis-how-a-372-million-loss-built-a-65-billion-quant-giant-b15c6bac91cd> - but it was decided that the decision to build up the exposure was collectively taken, and so it wouldn’t be fair to blame him alone.
That decision was actually quite typical of DE Shaw's management style – even before its founder stepped back in 2001 to concentrate on biomedical research, it was always quite a collegiate place, with a culture of executives “stress testing” one another’s bets. Part of the point of recruiting people with quirky educational backgrounds seems to have been a desire to avoid the kind of intellectual monoculture that leads to groupthink and blind spots. And even to this day, if an idea survives this kind of internal debate, DE Shaw is not scared of putting billions into a single trade.
Which, in turn, goes to explain one of the other cultural quirks and idiosyncrasies of DE Shaw – its extreme degree of secretiveness, even by the standards of hedge funds. Job candidates and employees agree not to share confidential information during interviews, and you have to agree to confidentiality terms if you get an offer. Clients are not encouraged to ask too many questions; with some justification, the company seems to think that its long term track record of investment returns ought to be all the answers that anyone needs.
That does seem to put a bit of strain on the client relationships. At present, DE Shaw is asking its investors to pay up for the cost of installing AI compute, while also increasing its lockup period to up to four years. And they are opening an internal fund for their best ideas, which employees will get preferential access to.
The internal fund looks like a defensive move aimed at helping to keep DE Shaw competitive for top talent with other legendary trading operations like RenTech, but that also underlines a problem of longevity. They need to recruit tomorrow’s star quants (and poets, philosophers, etc) because the original generation are getting old (or rather, getting rich – Stone is only in his 50s) and retiring. One consultant has already downgraded Shaw from “best in industry “ to merely “above average”.
So, the challenge is to maintain the quirky, secretive and collegiate culture of the fund for a new generation. Let’s hope that they manage it; it’s good for the industry for some places to be a bit weird.
Elsewhere, the new public statement from Binance <https://x.com/binance/status/2117626126214504729> about the multi-billion dollar hacking attack might contain some bad news for bankers, and particularly for techies working at financial institutions. According to the company, part of the preparation for the hack involved a particularly clever and sophisticated piece of “social engineering”.
An unfortunate Binance employee only known as “Engineer B” was approached on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone who seemed credible in offering him a job. After first- and second-round video interviews, the candidate was given an “exercise” which involved downloading some files onto his computer. These files apparently included a bunch of malicious code, which later executed “a series of unauthorised activities”.
It’s bad enough that everyone now has to be suspicious that every recruiter might be a global master criminal. But also – banks now have a security reason to want to prevent their employees from interviewing anywhere else, as well as all of the normal reasons. We can expect tougher controls on the use of work laptops, and stricter policies on communication with recruiters. It’s not just Binance who were the victims here.
Meanwhile …
Rich Handler has been in India, talking about launching an asset management venture and about hiring more staff. He’s also potentially there to steady the ship and show the employees some love after the departure of veteran country head Aashish Agarwal. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-03/jefferies-ceo-visits-india-as-us-firm-eyes-expansion-hiring>)
Merging UBS with Morgan Stanley has a certain kind of logic to it – expanding wealth management franchises, significant overlap and cost synergies, reuniting Ted Pick with Colm Kelleher. But it’s also got a lot of problems – overlapping clients and negative revenue synergies, the biggest integration problems in history and, quite possibly, opening up old wounds for Ted and Colm. (Breakingviews <https://www.breakingviews.com/columns/big-view/morgan-stanley-is-dubious-saviour-ubs-2026-11-03/>)
The thing about trade secrets being secret is that it’s often quite difficult to know how important they are, and whether they’re worth keeping secret in the first place. Richard Ho, formerly of trading firm Headland Technologies, is on trial for allegedly misappropriating the code for some algorithmic strategies. But, while Headland claims they spent as much as $1bn on developing those strategies, Ho’s defence team seem to be saying that they’re actually commonly known concepts of no economic significance. The case continues. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-03/quant-trader-s-criminal-trial-to-spotlight-secretive-industry?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261103&utm_campaign=author_3487187&leadSource=uverify%20wall>)
BNP Paribas is “creating an integrated Investment Banking platform bringing together Sectors, M&A, Debt Markets ⁠and Equity Capital Markets”, in the hope that this will bring the banking side of its Corporate and Investment Banking division closer to the success of its equities trading operation. (Reuters <https://creating%20an%20integrated%20Investment%20Banking%20platform%20bringing%20together%20Sectors,%20M&A,%20Debt%20Markets%20⁠and%20​Equity%20Capital%20Markets>)
All the fund managers and bankers who thought they were being clever by leaving London for tax breaks in Milan are now feeling a bit “Hotel California”, as the Meloni government proposes a 26% “exit tax” on expatriates who accrued profits under a favourable tax regime if they later leave. (FT <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-03/one-credit-fund-dodged-radiant-world-by-asking-to-check-invoices?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261103&utm_campaign=author_22490032>)
“The same qualities that we saw in you will no doubt serve you well at other firms who will be lucky to have you”. The plight of high flying law graduates who thought they had a prestigious associate job at Weil Gotschal and then very suddenly didn’t. (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/these-associates-had-a-golden-ticket-to-big-lawuntil-weil-gotshal-collapsed-2c2f7e86?mod=mhp>)
