item.title: The sudden shrivelling of the SocGen fixed income business
item.description:
It's SocGen results day and if you work in equities sales and trading sun is shining there with fervent zest. If you work in fixed income sales and trading, it is not.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
SocGen's figures show that its fixed income sales and trading revenues have shrivelled to just 28.3% of the combined revenues in equities and fixed income trading businesses after falling 21% year-on-year in the third quarter. Equities sales and trading revenues at SocGen rose 46% over the same period, driven partly by the consolidation of Bernstein's business in the US.
Many banks did not have a strong third quarter in fixed income trading but SocGen had the worst of the lot. Worse, even, than Bank of America </news/bofa-q3-2026> (-17%). Worse than Barclays </news/barclays-fixed-income-traders-are-getting-bigger-bonuses-at-just-the-wrong-time>(-19%). Worse than Deutsche Bank </news/deutsche-bank-q3-26-fixed-income>(-11% when FIC financing is excluded).
What went wrong? It's not entirely clear, but SocGen said today that activity has been lower in rates trading. European rates trading was presumably to blame given that this is where SocGen's hard-driving CEO Slawomir Krupa said the business was focused earlier this year. Unexpected gyrations </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up> in French government bonds may not have helped.
The decline meant that fixed income sales and trading revenues fell to the lowest they've been as a proportion of the total since at least 2022. Nine months ago, Krupa noted that the ratio was typically split 60:40 between equities and fixed income.
Fixed income's shrivelled status at the French bank follows the departure of Francisco "Chico" Oliveira in July. </news/francisco-oliveira>Oliveira was hired in 2025 with a mandate to pursue SocGen's "ambition" to grow the fixed income business, and flow trading in particular.
That appears to have been quietly set aside. During SocGen's strategy presentation in September, Krupa said the bank will now be growing its fixed income offering "beyond the flow business, and we will build on our strong origination capabilities to expand credit distribution” instead.

item.title: Morning Coffee: The dealmaker who turned out to be bigger than his firm. Deutsche Bank and BNP Paribas traders did very well
item.description:
They say that there is no “I” in “team”. But there are two of them in “private equity”, two in “billings” and there’s even one on in “Weil, Gotshal & Manges”. Or at least, there was; despite having up until recently been a top Wall Street law firm with $2.1bn in revenue, Weil, Gotsal's management have reportedly hired <https://www.wsj.com/pro/bankruptcy/weil-gotshal-taps-alixpartners-to-steer-wind-down-c51b561f> restructuring firm Alix Partners to advise on winding the firm up.
It seems that the catalyst for the firm’s rapid disassembly was the loss of Michael Aiello, the head of its corporate department and a significant dealmaker in his own right, who had advised on more than $110bn in M&A transactions <https://www.weil.com/articles/weil-partners-named-finalists-in-the-american-lawyers-2026-industry-awards>. Aiello decided to go to Cravath, Swaine & Moore in September, and this seems to have destabilised the whole partnership.
According to commentators on the legal services industry, Weil had begun to fall behind its competitors in headcount and profits, as a result of paying out profits rather than reinvesting them in growth. This made the firm vulnerable to having its attorneys poached by competitors, as anyone who was making good money there could be credibly promised even bigger opportunities at a practice with more clients.
There was apparently a certain amount of strategic disagreement between the partners over whether Weil should go for growth or remain small, which contributed to private equity partner Ramona Nee’s decision to turn down the chief partner role she’d been offered, according to the Wall Street Journal. It can’t have been easy to manage such a conflict, particularly in the knowledge that nearly everyone involved might have had an offer to go somewhere else in their back pockets.
Aiello’s exit followed that of Chris Machera, co-head of private equity, who left for Paul Weiss in August. David Avery-Gee followed Aiello out of the door in September. As many as 60 partners and associates left Weil over the summer and early autumn. The management committee tried to find a merger partner, but the talks fell through.
This sort of thing happens much less often in banking, and it demonstrates one of the key differences between banks and other parts of the financial profession. Banks have capital, liabilities and infrastructure costs. This means that they can, and sometimes do, go bust, but it also means that there is an actual business there, distinct from its employees. With a law firm (or a consultancy, or an advisory boutique), the people are literally all there is. The company only holds together as long as the personal relationships do. And there isn’t much to be acquired in a crisis; the competitors that Weil approached might have reasoned that there was no reason to give up any equity in a combination when they could just wait a few weeks and recruit the individuals that they wanted.
It also means that leadership and culture are even more important in these kinds of firms. Michael Aiello might not have realised that he was the load-bearing brick, but clearly a lot of his colleagues regarded him that way. It’s frequently said that no individual player is bigger than the team, but that’s not always true.
Elsewhere, it’s been interesting to see that, although the bankers of Europe don’t have the megadeals and tech IPOs which drove profits for their American competitors, the traders of Europe can hold their heads high <https://It's%20a%20take%20https:/www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-28/deutsche-bank-bnp-show-europe-can-out-do-wall-street-traders>. In fact, the equity traders at BNP Paribas </news/bnp-q3-2026> saw revenues up 50% on last year, compared to an average of 43% for Wall Street (Barclays were almost as strong, up 47%). Deutsche Bank’s </news/deutsche-bank-q3-26-fixed-income> fixed income desk did better than the bulge bracket in tough conditions <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-28/deutsche-bank-s-fixed-income-trading-meets-estimate-in-quarter>, and Christian Sewing seemed to be quite bullish for the near future, saying that the current RoE target should be achieved and that this isn’t “the end game, not at all”.
It would probably be excessively optimistic to hope that this might be reflected in bonuses; European traders are likely to have to make a contribution to the capital markets and advisory compensation pools, while American traders will hope to take a share in the deal wealth. But it’s nice to have some bragging rights, for once in a while.
Meanwhile …
William Evarts has a law degree, and a lot of experience with refinancing transactions for companies seeking to avoid bankruptcy. But he isn’t a lawyer by trade, so it’s quite interesting to see him move from PJT Partners to be head of the “liability management” practice at Sidley Austin. One lawyer commented that this sort of move might become more likely as the top law firms are able to pay more, and need people who can drive business volumes. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/84da55e7-f544-4c80-81fc-02fa166454fa?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
You wouldn’t think that someone working for a top multi-strategy hedge fund would let a chatbot pick their stocks, but at a recent summit, leaders at Citadel, Bridgewater and Man Group agreed that there is a danger of “cognitive capture”, when teams grow to trust their AI sidekicks a bit too much. (Business Insider <https://www.businessinsider.com/hedge-funds-citadel-and-bridgewater-handling-ai-2026-10>)
Hamza Lemssouguer is not used to playing defence rather than offence, and the European junk bond market </news/european-high-yield>is not used to his fund slowing down its trading rather than bidding aggressively across the space. It seems that the whole sector is worried that if the standout star of the last five years is having a tough time, can anyone make money at all? (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-28/star-hedge-fund-trader-lemssouguer-s-woes-at-arini-roil-european-junk-bonds>)
Everyone with a net worth of more than £1bn in the UK is going to be assigned a personal “customer compliance manager” by the tax authorities, which sounds like a role combining concierge service with implicit threat. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/c8c12f19-6e23-4e43-926a-463ba0bcc9d0?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Some private equity firms are trying to include clauses in buyouts which say that if the company is disrupted by AI, then that’s an act of God or force majeure and the default shouldn’t count. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/acts-of-god-meet-acts-of-ai-in-private-equity-s-new-debt-play?utm_source=www.shortsqueez.co&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=mbappe-vs-china&_bhlid=595ddbdca805ce3b18ae57417ec3727f655e4628>)
Even a frontier model with a state of the art agentic harness seems to make mistakes like “leaving Erling Haaland on the bench” when you try to use it to win at fantasy football. (WIRED <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-28/star-hedge-fund-trader-lemssouguer-s-woes-at-arini-roil-european-junk-bonds>)

item.title: Only Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley and Nomura didn't mention cost cuts in Q4
item.description:
Most top US banks and most top European banks have now announced their third quarter results. It was not a bad quarter, particularly if you had the good fortune to work in prime broking, equities sales and trading or equity capital markets (ECM) - Morgan Stanley’s ECM business excepted.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
The chart at the bottom of this page shows performance by bank and by business. The final three months of this year aren’t expected to go badly. Nor, however, are they expected to go extremely well.
Markets revenues are expected to fall in line with standard seasonality in Q4, but Morgan Stanley and Standard Chartered have both flagged weakness in Asia. Morgan Stanley said Asian trading volumes “were drying up” in September, and Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters pointed to “particularly weak equity markets in Asia” so far this quarter.
Meanwhile the investment banking pipeline looks less buoyant than earlier in the year at Goldman Sachs, where the backlog has slipped since the end of 2025, and at Citi, which expects fees to come in below 2026’s near-record pace. JPMorgan said its pipeline slowed in the second half of September. It’s “like an accordion”, said Jamie Dimon. - It can suddenly expand; it can also suddenly contract.
In the circumstances, it’s perhaps unsurprising that banks are still focused on cutting costs and maximising efficiencies. UBS has a further $500m of cuts to make in the fourth quarter based upon its target. HSBC has $100m of its $2bn of cuts to go. BNP Paribas’s 2026 guidance implies another €160m of cost savings in Q4. Citi brought forward $500m of investment and severance spending into the second half, about half of which is still to come. Barclays expects to spend around $400m in Q4 on cost actions involving the removal of 5,000 jobs, of which 60% will be in support functions. Standard Chartered is wrapping up its Fit for Growth cost programme, on which it has spent $377m so far this year.
Deutsche Bank’s CFO Raja Akram said yesterday its €21.3bn full-year cost guidance includes “severance charges”, and that it has “a few more actions we can execute in the fourth quarter that would actually be a benefit to us in 2027 and 2028”. However, Raja was referring to the private bank rather than the investment bank. CEO Christian Sewing said AI and “workforce” measures offer further cost upside, with details promised alongside full-year results in January.
Not all the extracted costs will come from lost jobs, but it could be a busy few months for HR teams. As at Barclays, middle and back office </news/front-office-middle-office-back-office-banking> staff are most at risk from “efficiency driven by AI.”
Some banks didn’t flag cost cutting in their third quarter results, though. Neither Goldman Sachs, nor JPMorgan, nor Morgan Stanley, nor Nomura mentioned cost-cutting plans in the coming quarter. This doesn’t mean they won’t cut costs. It does, perhaps, mean that jobs will be safest there until at least Christmas.

item.title: Evercore will very probably pay $1.2m+ this year
item.description:
While the big US banks reported their Q3 earnings some time ago (and European banks are doing so currently), its boutique banks </news/boutique-investment-banks> have only just started reporting theirs. Among the first, as usual, is Evercore.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Evercore did very well in Q3, on top of its performance in the first half of the year. Q3 net revenues for 2026 were up 12% on the same period in 2025; net revenues for the first nine months of the year were up 38% across the same period.
Headcount and compensation, in turn, grew. Evercore had 2,835 people at the end of Q3 2026; a year ago, it had 2,525, a 13% increase. Its senior managing director (SMD) count also increased by 13%, from 207 to 233. That’s proportional, of course, and also flies somewhat in the face of the expected wisdom from Lazard </news/lazard-q3-2026> and the likes, which expect deal teams to shrink, and the proportion of dealmakers to junior bankers to increase. Clearly, that hasn’t happened at Evercore.
Pay was a standout. The firm has earmarked compensation of $810k per head in the first nine months of the year, up from the $669k it paid on average in the first nine months of 2025. In the chart below, we found that the nine-month-to-year-end compensation ratio was around 1.5. If that pattern holds in 2026 too, average pay should clear the $1.2m mark. Not bad at all.
The firm noted that it had hired six SMDs in Q3; Dylan Tornay from Citi’s equity capital markets team, John Pissanos from JPMorgan’s healthcare banking team, John Song and Jean Stack from Baird, John Vaske from Ducera, and Philip von Malsen-Plessen, UBS’ vice-chair of global banking in EMEA.

item.title: 25-year-old London bankers on £200k do not want to pay more tax
item.description:
If you earn £200k ($266k) in the UK, you may yet be asked to explain yourself </news/nik-storonsky-revolut>to His Majesty's Revenue and Customs. Associate level </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> bankers in London typically earn more than this, but ahead of today's budget, young bankers would like to let it be known that they do not feel rich.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Starting salaries for 22 year-old junior bankers in M&A in the UK are circa £75k </news/2023/10/london-investment-bank-pay>at major banks. </news/the-top-tier-banks-are-goldman-sachs-jp-morgan-and-morgan-stanley-except-for-here> These are supplemented by bonuses of circa £30k (or more, depending upon the year). Three years later, as full associates, the same juniors can expect salaries of over £100k and equivalent bonuses.
This puts them in the top 1% of UK income tax payers. But juniors in London banks today say they do not feel rich. They do not want to pay more tax. They suggest that managing directors (MDs) should be targeted instead.
"Base starting salary after tax isn’t really at the level to support renting on your own anywhere in Central London," says one LSE graduate. "So you need to live further out or to accept a longer commute. Or you need to stay at home with your parents for much longer."
Without family money, she says the only way to afford a house now is to wait and to save bonuses for a deposit. But junior bankers educated at UK universities who have the notorious Plan 2 student loans pay a 71% marginal rate of tax on income between £100k and £125k. If they have a Master's qualification and additional Plan 2 loans, the marginal rate is 77%. "It’s very tough," says the LSE graduate. "There's a massive disconnect between the pace of inflation on housing versus starting salaries which have barely moved in 15 years."
One 28 year-old associate says he's just bought a London apartment with help from his family. "I'm not even sure the after-tax proceeds from my next bonus will be sufficient to cover the renovation costs alone. Despite earning what would objectively be considered a very good salary, the taxes, cost of living and property prices in London make it difficult to feel particularly wealthy." Another junior said he's worried about paying his large mortgage if interest rates rise.
Instead of taxing junior bankers, junior bankers suggest taxing senior bankers. "My MD told me he was buying his 4th house," says one. "I pointed out that this is why 25 year-old bankers can't afford to buy a place any more. We are having to compete with your generation that racked up a lot of cheap real estate."
He tells us that young bankers look at MDs and see that they have lives very different to their own and that it was always thus. "People aged 40-45 in banking were able to buy cheap houses and so today they have a lot of security. Relative to purchasing power they had much higher salaries and bonuses than we do now."
If taxes are going to rise, he suggests they should therefore rise on MDs. "Every junior person in finance/law/medicine, anyone aged 25-35 in London, feels stretched." MDs are "surfing on the back of the new generation," he adds. "These people really can't be on the same tax bracket as the 20-30 year olds earning £145k and trying to make a living.
Taxes on £5m houses also need to rise, he suggests. Some offer a word of caution, though. "MDs already pay 45%+ of their earnings in taxes. The idea that someone should be taxed even more simply because they have worked their way up to a highly paid position seems fundamentally misguided," says another associate. "These are highly skilled, internationally mobile professionals who can often earn comparable salaries in other financial centres."

item.title: Dutch electronic trading firm picks up a French salesperson in Hong Kong
item.description:
The electronic trading industry </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-an-electronic-trading-firm> might be all excited about trading and market making compute </news/the-impending-boom-of-compute-trading-markets-everyone-is-keeping-their-cards-close-to-their-chest> these days, but sometimes, you need the classics, like selling derivative products to institutions. The sort of trade your grandfather would recognize, really.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Coline Gerard joined electronic trading firm Optiver’s derivatives institutional sales team earlier this month in Hong Kong. She joined the firm from Goldman Sachs, where she worked for eight years across Paris, London, and most recently Hong Kong.
Joining at the same time as her was Patrick Jacob, a former Nomura equity derivatives salesperson, although seemingly not French. Jacob is also the founder of Labret, a Hong Kong-based piercing and jewelry brand. Both will be reporting to Stéphane Martin, who is possibly French, and is certainly Optiver’s head of derivatives institutional sales in APAC, based in Singapore.
Optiver has been growing recently. Bloomberg reported <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/high-frequency-trader-optiver-seeks-900-million-debt-package> last week that the firm was seeking to raise $900m to finance an expansion - via $700m in debt and a $200m revolver - although that was on hold due to market uncertainty and the US elections, among other things. Bloomberg said that the arrangement had no clear target date, however, and might even be cancelled.
Optiver did not respond to a request for comment. The firm does not seem to have any open job postings in Hong Kong - while it does have three in Taipei, four in Mumbai, eight in Singapore, and 27 in Sydney. It does not have any open positions in its derivatives team either, except for an engineering role.

item.title: Balyasny's big London equity derivatives guy appears to have gone to Millennium
item.description:
It's nearly Halloween and appropriately enough, Max Witcher is on the move.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Witcher is understood to have left hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>Balyasny Asset Management (BAM) in London and to be en route to Millennium where he will run a new pod.
Witcher's official whereabouts are, however, cloaked in mystery. He didn't respond to a request to comment for this article. Nor did Balyasny. Millennium declined to comment. Only the FCA Register sheds some light on the situation: it says he was deregistered from Balyasny Asset Management's UK entity at the end of July. He has yet to officially work his magic elsewhere.
Witcher is a delta one trader. Although hedge funds are casting aside </news/hedge-funds-hired-too-many-morons-and-other-unpopular-opinions-as-the-industry-pukes-p-ms> macro </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up>and credit </news/european-high-yield> portfolio managers, delta one traders who cover the ever-expanding universe of index rebalancing, ETF arbitrage, dividend trading and equity financing are still hot.
Witcher is understood to be among the best. Before BAM he was at LMR. Before LMR he was at JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs. At Balyasny he was part of star PM Dan Avery's </news/dan-avery-balyasny> team. Avery is still at BAM and his pod is thought to be one of the top performing there this year.
Curiously, the FCA Register shows Witcher registered at Millennium before - for a brief three month period during the pandemic of 2020. Then he vanished from the London scene and reappeared at LMR nine months later. It's not clear which realm he occupied during the interval. Gardening leave may explain the absence.

item.title: BNP Paribas' 2030 priorities: more AI, less offshoring, same buildings
item.description:
With European Q3 reporting season well under way, mixed results have come through. Three banks have reported this morning: UBS </news/ubs-q3-2026>, which didn’t do so well, Deutsche Bank </news/deutsche-bank-q3-26-fixed-income>, which did a bit better, and BNP Paribas, which is doing something else entirely.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
BNP’s investor presentation detailed its substantial savings plan over the next three years. Its rather ambitious target – to save €4bn, including €2.4bn in support function spend – was primarily based around five key line items.
The bank intends to save on two primary things: “shoring”, presumably both off- and near-shoring, and “organization simplification” and “renunciation”. That means making cuts. It probably means making a lot of cuts, in fact, given that the bank intends to increase spending – on “process optimization”, which is a bit vague, and on AI, which is rather explicit. To that end, the bank has launched a five-year partnership with Google ‘s Gemini. It has also said that “external spend,” which includes real estate, would remain flat by 2030.
It’s a bold plan. In the firm’s Q2 investor call, CEO Jean-Laurent Bonnafé said that more than 80% of the savings available were “clearly identified”, and a quarter of them should come by Q1 2027. The firm intended to “pool and streamline” its application portfolio, “amplify the use of AI,” and “simplify” the organization. He also said BNP was targeting a 50% cost-income ratio over time, well down from 60% it forecast for 2026. It was 59% in the first half of the year, and 58% in Q3. Perhaps the bank expects costs to increase in Q4.
While BNP hasn’t been having a great year </news/how-did-banks-do-q2-2026>, its Q3 was somewhat better; equities sales & trading revenue was up by 50% on the third quarter of 2025, which was the second-best result of the banks we’ve covered this year, and its fixed income, currencies, and commodities revenue was down just 0.6%, on par with Goldman Sachs and well ahead of Barclays </news/barclays-fixed-income-traders-are-getting-bigger-bonuses-at-just-the-wrong-time>, Bank of America </news/bofa-q3-2026>, and the likes.
Investment banking – which includes lending and transaction revenue – is performing a bit better, especially debt capital markets (DCM). The bank noted that its Americas banking revenue was growing by double digits, “particularly DCM, acquisition finance, securitisation and infrastructure finance.” Capital markets were also strong in APAC. Market intelligence firm Dealogic noted that it increased its global banking market share by around 0.1%.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Elite quant finance students are on $800k as AI labs want them too. The tech jobs safe from AI firings
item.description:
Last month, we noted that something startling </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street> had happened to pay for the finest quantitative finance graduates. For a couple of decades now, quantitative finance has been trying to deal with a very particular problem – how to attract the top quants, when Silicon Valley can offer similar salaries, more social cachet and the chance of a generational IPO? For a couple of years, it looked like the problem might have been solved, when Big Tech started to become as unpopular as Big Banking. But then the AI boom began, and while they’re not exactly universally popular, the frontier labs are able to provide elite researchers with the feeling of being at the leading edge of a scientific revolution, rather than trying to shave a few microseconds off trading latency.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
So, “academic outreach <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/ai-talent-war-has-quant-firms-racing-to-fund-phds-build-labs?taid=6ae0aae51d3fbb0001b048a3&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>” professionals – that specialised bit of the talent acquisition industry which deals with the very bright indeed – have their work cut out for them. What can they offer that the frontier labs can’t? Or perhaps more realisitically, how close can they get to matching the AI offer?
Obviously, money is part of the package. In line with our reporting, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/ai-talent-war-has-quant-firms-racing-to-fund-phds-build-labs> says first year hires with PhDs in hot areas like machine learning can ask for compensation packages as high as $800k. And it only gets better from there – there are quite a few quant firms now where the average comp </news/jump-trading-joins-the-1m-per-head-club-in-london-as-average-pay-rose-55> is in seven figures. Lots of trading firms prefer to stay private rather than IPOing, but that doesn’t mean that they can’t compete financially.
And money isn’t everything, particularly to genius mathematicians. While normal bankers can be motivated by cars and watches, the greatest luxury for a top quant is to be given a lot of time and freedom to do maths, and elite intellectual company to do it with.
So firms like Qube, G-Research and CFM, a Paris hedge fund founded by a professor, are building labs and sponsoring PhDs with “complete academic freedom” and “no expectation of work applicable to finance”. The idea seems to be partly that this selfless contribution will cast a positive light on the employer brand. But more subtly, it means that top PhDs and postdocs will continually be seeing people at global academic conferences who are proudly wearing the swag of a quant trading firm, and who have “technical staff member” (the new cool title) on their business cards. That’s likely to give them a bit of conference that if they were to join a quant firm, they would still be able to participate in the global research community, and wouldn’t necessarily have to give up their dreams of a Fields Medal.
To some extent, it’s a bit sneaky to try and give young students the idea that trading is all about intellectual challenge. The life of most quants involves a lot more perspiration than inspiration – a surprising proportion of the job has always been the checking of datasets for bank holiday dates. But the challenge is real – as Alex Davies of Jump Trading puts it, the difference between market models and language models is that if you achieve a perfect translation, your competitors don’t start changing the language to make it harder for you. The competitive element is what makes finance so frustrating and fascinating, and in the end, it’s likely to be the recruiters’ secret weapon in the war for PhD talent.
Elsewhere, Microsoft has launched a “buyout offer <https://www.semafor.com/article/10/27/2026/microsofts-buyout-offer-to-employees-shows-which-tech-jobs-matter>” (an invitation to take voluntary redundancy) to a quarter of its employees. A similar offer made in July <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/microsoft-to-offer-buyouts-to-60-000-workers-in-latest-cost-cut?srnd=homepage-americas> resulted in 8,750 headcount reductions; the company apparently expects “far fewer” to go this time. So perhaps the interesting thing to look at is not who the offer is being made to, but who is specifically excluded from its scope.
It’s not as simple as “AI versus not-AI” – people working on CoPilot are eligible. The core revenue generating product staff working on Windows are eligible, as is the finance function. The employees who are excluded from redundancy are those working on data centres, cybersecurity and quantum computing. (And sales and marketing, but this is quite normal – companies don’t cut sales functions unless things have really got bad).
Microsoft describes this as “employees who are engaged on the hard problems that it’s trying to solve”. Which means that the read through to finance jobs is a bit difficult to assess - apart from cybersecurity, the banks have different problems.
Meanwhile …
It’s not clear exactly what’s going on, and the company hasn’t commented, but news organisations are reporting that Weil Gotschal have retained a lawyer of their own, after the rash of senior partner departures may have left them in need of restructuring services. When the most valuable assets are people, resignations can be contagious. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/69ccfcb0-3f5e-4b77-9e04-a386e827b872?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Sequoia, Citadel Securities and OpenAI have teamed up to sponsor a poker tournament for university students and recent graduates. Not to play themselves, but to code, from scratch, a “pokerbot” capable of playing 10,000 hands of no-limit Texas Hold’em. (pokerbot.sequoiacap.com <https://pokerbot.sequoiacap.com/>)
The New Zealand poaching case between Barrenjoey and Jarden continues. Bankers have been accused of “behaving poorly”, which is quite a strong condemnatory statement in context. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/jarden-bankers-acted-as-insider-in-barrenjoey-raid-court-told>)
After a short “AI Winter” in which it looked as if business insight was about to be commoditised by chatbots, it looks as if the management consultancy industry is back on the front foot. Base pay is up at McKinsey, BCG and Bain for the first time since 2022, revenues are growing again and McKinsey aims to hire 12% more graduates this year than last. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/dcfaf62f-497d-4db0-bb2d-a55e0b749750?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
The Baltic Exchange is running into huge problems with maintaining a crucial shipping price index (with billions of dollars of derivatives written on it). Conditions in the Strait of Hormuz mean that pricing is now based on rumours in WhatsApp groups, and one energy trading firm is complaining to the FCA. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/sinokor-tanker-tycoon-s-whatsapp-messages-influence-oil-transport-prices?srnd=homepage-americas>)
Some people think that they lose all respect for you if you’re constantly giving them treats. Others say that this is garbage, and you just need to firmly impress on them who’s the boss. Who knew that the world of dog training had so much in common with managing junior bankers? (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/tough-love-vs-nonstop-treatsthe-civil-war-over-dog-training-54dd190a?mod=mhp>)

item.title: Morning Coffee: Elite quant finance students are on $800k as AI labs want them too. The tech jobs safe from AI firings
item.description:
Last month, we noted that something startling </news/pay-for-electronic-trading-graduates-is-soaring-1m-at-hrt-850k-at-jane-street> had happened to pay for the finest quantitative finance graduates. For a couple of decades now, quantitative finance has been trying to deal with a very particular problem – how to attract the top quants, when Silicon Valley can offer similar salaries, more social cachet and the chance of a generational IPO? For a couple of years, it looked like the problem might have been solved, when Big Tech started to become as unpopular as Big Banking. But then the AI boom began, and while they’re not exactly universally popular, the frontier labs are able to provide elite researchers with the feeling of being at the leading edge of a scientific revolution, rather than trying to shave a few microseconds off trading latency.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
So, “academic outreach <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/ai-talent-war-has-quant-firms-racing-to-fund-phds-build-labs?taid=6ae0aae51d3fbb0001b048a3&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>” professionals – that specialised bit of the talent acquisition industry which deals with the very bright indeed – have their work cut out for them. What can they offer that the frontier labs can’t? Or perhaps more realisitically, how close can they get to matching the AI offer?
Obviously, money is part of the package. In line with our reporting, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/ai-talent-war-has-quant-firms-racing-to-fund-phds-build-labs> says first year hires with PhDs in hot areas like machine learning can ask for compensation packages as high as $800k. And it only gets better from there – there are quite a few quant firms now where the average comp </news/jump-trading-joins-the-1m-per-head-club-in-london-as-average-pay-rose-55> is in seven figures. Lots of trading firms prefer to stay private rather than IPOing, but that doesn’t mean that they can’t compete financially.
And money isn’t everything, particularly to genius mathematicians. While normal bankers can be motivated by cars and watches, the greatest luxury for a top quant is to be given a lot of time and freedom to do maths, and elite intellectual company to do it with.
So firms like Qube, G-Research and CFM, a Paris hedge fund founded by a professor, are building labs and sponsoring PhDs with “complete academic freedom” and “no expectation of work applicable to finance”. The idea seems to be partly that this selfless contribution will cast a positive light on the employer brand. But more subtly, it means that top PhDs and postdocs will continually be seeing people at global academic conferences who are proudly wearing the swag of a quant trading firm, and who have “technical staff member” (the new cool title) on their business cards. That’s likely to give them a bit of conference that if they were to join a quant firm, they would still be able to participate in the global research community, and wouldn’t necessarily have to give up their dreams of a Fields Medal.
To some extent, it’s a bit sneaky to try and give young students the idea that trading is all about intellectual challenge. The life of most quants involves a lot more perspiration than inspiration – a surprising proportion of the job has always been the checking of datasets for bank holiday dates. But the challenge is real – as Alex Davies of Jump Trading puts it, the difference between market models and language models is that if you achieve a perfect translation, your competitors don’t start changing the language to make it harder for you. The competitive element is what makes finance so frustrating and fascinating, and in the end, it’s likely to be the recruiters’ secret weapon in the war for PhD talent.
Elsewhere, Microsoft has launched a “buyout offer <https://www.semafor.com/article/10/27/2026/microsofts-buyout-offer-to-employees-shows-which-tech-jobs-matter>” (an invitation to take voluntary redundancy) to a quarter of its employees. A similar offer made in July <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/microsoft-to-offer-buyouts-to-60-000-workers-in-latest-cost-cut?srnd=homepage-americas> resulted in 8,750 headcount reductions; the company apparently expects “far fewer” to go this time. So perhaps the interesting thing to look at is not who the offer is being made to, but who is specifically excluded from its scope.
It’s not as simple as “AI versus not-AI” – people working on CoPilot are eligible. The core revenue generating product staff working on Windows are eligible, as is the finance function. The employees who are excluded from redundancy are those working on data centres, cybersecurity and quantum computing. (And sales and marketing, but this is quite normal – companies don’t cut sales functions unless things have really got bad).
Microsoft describes this as “employees who are engaged on the hard problems that it’s trying to solve”. Which means that the read through to finance jobs is a bit difficult to assess - apart from cybersecurity, the banks have different problems.
Meanwhile …
It’s not clear exactly what’s going on, and the company hasn’t commented, but news organisations are reporting that Weil Gotschal have retained a lawyer of their own, after the rash of senior partner departures may have left them in need of restructuring services. When the most valuable assets are people, resignations can be contagious. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/69ccfcb0-3f5e-4b77-9e04-a386e827b872?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
Sequoia, Citadel Securities and OpenAI have teamed up to sponsor a poker tournament for university students and recent graduates. Not to play themselves, but to code, from scratch, a “pokerbot” capable of playing 10,000 hands of no-limit Texas Hold’em. (pokerbot.sequoiacap.com <https://pokerbot.sequoiacap.com/>)
The New Zealand poaching case between Barrenjoey and Jarden continues. Bankers have been accused of “behaving poorly”, which is quite a strong condemnatory statement in context. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/jarden-bankers-acted-as-insider-in-barrenjoey-raid-court-told>)
After a short “AI Winter” in which it looked as if business insight was about to be commoditised by chatbots, it looks as if the management consultancy industry is back on the front foot. Base pay is up at McKinsey, BCG and Bain for the first time since 2022, revenues are growing again and McKinsey aims to hire 12% more graduates this year than last. (FT <https://www.ft.com/content/dcfaf62f-497d-4db0-bb2d-a55e0b749750?syn-25a6b1a6=1>)
The Baltic Exchange is running into huge problems with maintaining a crucial shipping price index (with billions of dollars of derivatives written on it). Conditions in the Strait of Hormuz mean that pricing is now based on rumours in WhatsApp groups, and one energy trading firm is complaining to the FCA. (Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/sinokor-tanker-tycoon-s-whatsapp-messages-influence-oil-transport-prices?srnd=homepage-americas>)
Some people think that they lose all respect for you if you’re constantly giving them treats. Others say that this is garbage, and you just need to firmly impress on them who’s the boss. Who knew that the world of dog training had so much in common with managing junior bankers? (WSJ <https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/tough-love-vs-nonstop-treatsthe-civil-war-over-dog-training-54dd190a?mod=mhp>)

item.title: Deutsche Bank's distressed debt traders are not receiving a CFO shoutout this quarter
item.description:
This time last year, distressed debt traders at Deutsche Bank were having a great time. CJ Lanktree </news/cj-lanktree-deutsche-bank>had just returned from Solus Asset Management to head the distressed business, which made around $200m in the third quarter of 2025, prompting a special shoutout from the CFO in the results call.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
This year, things are a bit different. Deutsche Bank’s distressed debt traders are not thriving. Fixed income sales and trading revenues at the bank, excluding financing revenues, fell 11% year-on-year in the third quarter, to €1.43bn, and were up just 2% in the first nine months. For this, Deutsche blamed “the non-recurrence of a very strong credit trading performance in the prior-year quarter, specifically within the distressed business.”
There are new favourites instead. Emerging markets traders got a shoutout from CFO Raja Akram this year. Fixed income financing is also doing well - revenues there were up 10%. Financing hedge fund trades and others through the prime broking team now accounts for 40% of Deutsche's total fixed income revenues, up from 35% last year.
They may still get paid. Deutsche Bank spent an extra 3% on compensation in its investment bank in the third quarter, amounting to an additional 6% per head by our calculation after back office cuts earlier this year. Some of that may go to the equity capital markets bankers who increased revenues 63% in Q3.
If you want to work for Deutsche, the bank is hiring. 203 people were added to front office functions in the investment bank in Q3, even as 464 operations staff were cut over the past year. Additions earlier this year included new emerging market traders like Thomas Fitzpatrick and Christopher Staudt <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-28/deutsche-bank-deepens-emerging-market-rebuild-adds-two-traders> in New York. They may also get the big bonuses for 2026.

item.title: UBS's M&A bankers are doing terribly. $200m extra is being cut across the bank
item.description:
Like clockwork, a few weeks after the Americans, it’s Q3 reporting season for Europe’s investment banks. In England, Barclays was first </news/barclays-fixed-income-traders-are-getting-bigger-bonuses-at-just-the-wrong-time>, last week. Today, there are three: Deutsche Bank in Germany, BNP Paribas in France, and UBS in Switzerland.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
The headline figure, of course, is that UBS’ M&A bankers oversaw a nasty drop in revenue – down by 44% in Q3 of 2026 compared to Q3 of 2025. While banking revenue can be complicated by when exactly deals are booked etc., it’s still not a good result; banks such as JPMorgan </news/jpmorgan-q3-2026> and Morgan Stanley </news/morgan-stanley-thinks-goldman-sachs-traders-probably-did-well-in-the-third-quarter> are up 30% in the same period, while UBS’ main European competitors, Deutsche and Barclays </news/barclays-fixed-income-traders-are-getting-bigger-bonuses-at-just-the-wrong-time>, are up by 19% and 13%, respectively.
The Barclays comparison is particularly painful. UBS has spent years hiring from </news/ubs-bankers-are-wondering-whether-their-barclays-bosses-are-worth-it> the British bank, paying huge, allegedly guaranteed bonuses for “top performance” </news/it-s-ubs-bonus-day-we-re-not-shy-about-paying-for-top-performance>. That hasn’t materialized, and if anything, UBS has slid further and further down the banking league tables over the years, especially in North America, where a lot of the new Barclays veterans joined.
Probably unrelatedly, UBS has found some more cuts to make. “Additional efficiencies” being “identified” this quarter raised the firm’s cost savings target from $13.5bn to $13.7bn. Around $500m of those cuts are still due to occur in Q4.
Most of those savings are related to the Credit Suisse merger, of course. About 98% of ex-Credit Suisse apps are now out of use, and about 90% are “fully decommissioned”. By the end of the year, UBS aims to “materially complete” the wind-down and integration of IT infrastructure legal entities. It’s unclear what will happen to the ex-Credit Suisse people who have been maintaining that.
Elsewise, UBS didn’t do equally awfully. Equities trading revenue was up by 20% compared to Q3 of 2025, which was well behind peers like Goldman Sachs </news/prime-broking> (72%) up but at least better than Bank of America </news/bofa-q3-2026> or Citi </news/citi-m-a-bankers>, which were only up by 11% and 14%, respectively. There was one bright spot for UBS, however: its prime brokerage financing team, which it credited to most of its equities revenue increase.
Fixed income, currencies, and commodities (FICC) trading revenue, which was up 0.7% compared to Q3 of 2025, was possibly even an overperformance; the only bank that did better this results season was Citi, whose FICC traders were up by 4% in the same period.

item.title: DBS has a new MD in Singapore. He’s rather green, all things considered
item.description:
ESG isn’t what it used to be. Since the election in the US, environmental priorities have been on the back foot; the net zero banking alliance, which involved nine American and European banks, shut down last year <https://www.portfolio-institutional.co.uk/esg-hub/nzba-calls-it-a-day-with-the-end-of-operations/>, for example. Luckily, some parts of the world seem to be still holding the good fight to heart.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Thaddeus Tien joined DBS Bank in Singapore this month as global head of the firm’s energy, renewables, and infrastructure banking team. Tien joined the Singaporean bank from Natixis, which he joined less than a year and a half ago. Tien was at Barclays in Singapore for nearly a decade before that.
Tien’s role at DBS was previously held by Kelvin Wong, who became DBS’s chief sustainability officer (CSO) in May. Curiously, DBS’ previous CSO, Helge Muenkel, left DBS (and Singapore) to become head of climate & nature at Australian bank ANZ. Plenty of career opportunities ahead.
Tien will likely be pretty busy at DBS. The bank has been pushing into energy transition finance since it pledged in 2021 <https://www.dbs.com/newsroom/DBS_Bank_commits_to_zero_thermal_coal_exposure_by_2039> to cut its thermal coal exposure to zero by 2039. It’s even called itself <https://www.siew.gov.sg/media/5qs-interviews/detail/dbs-transition-finance-blueprint-for-accelerating-asias-energy-transformation> the “transition bank of Asia”, which is exciting.

item.title: Ex-Goldman Sachs MD turned hedge fund headhunter now works for a fund
item.description:
Henry Howell l </news/2023/04/goldman-sachs-to-hedge-fund>eft Goldman Sachs nearly seven years ago. Since then he has had a portfolio career of multiple jobs across headhunting, crypto, risk, and consulting. Now he is back with a fund full time.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Howell joined GemCorp Capital as global co-hed of business development and investor relations, based in London. In this role, GemCorp says he will be "building strategic relationships with investors and partners."
GemCorp Capital is an emerging markets investment firm focused mostly on private credit.
Howell will find some familiar faces there. The GemCorp founder is Atanas Bostandjiev, who was once Goldman's co-head of emerging markets for Central and Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa. GemCorp Capital's president is Carey Nemeth, a "great guy" </news/carey-nemeth-eisler>and former Goldman MD who was Eisler's COO and then briefly CEO of Eisler Capital in the US.
Howell also worked for Eisler, but only for a flash. He was in business development there for little over a year and left in 2021.

item.title: A 27-year-old investment banker left a tough team at Deutsche Bank and now look at him
item.description:
It's not necessarily easy to be a technology, media and telecoms (TMT) </news/technology-bankers>banker </news/highest-paid-bankers> at Deutsche Bank. Last time we looked, </news/deutsche-bank-s-london-tmt-juniors-keep-leaving-allegedly-due-to-overwork> juniors had been leaving the team run by Mathew Mathew </news/mathew-mathew-deutsche-bank>and Martin Blanquart due to what some told us were heavy workloads. Times may have changed, but one ex-member of the team suggests there are fine opportunities on offer to those who walk away.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
We have not spoken to William Hardy, who did not respond to a request to comment for this article, and nor have we confirmed his age, but by our reckoning he is aged either 27 or 28. Last December, he left Deutsche Bank's London office to become chief of staff at Omilia, a conversational intelligence company using AI. Now he is group CFO.
Hardy's ascent has not gone unnoticed among his former colleagues at DB. "He's probably one of the youngest CFOs in the UK," remarks one.
Being CFO at an AI company has the potential to be lucrative. In August, Omilia announced <https://omilia.com/resources/news/omilia-secures-67-million-in-series-b-funding-to-accelerate-global-expansion-of-its-agentic-cx-platform-for-large-enterprises/> a $67 million Series B funding round led by transatlantic software & AI specialist, Expedition Growth Capital. It has annual recurring revenues of over $60m and Taco Bell among its clients.
Other Deutsche Bank TMT juniors may therefore want to be like Hardy. In April, there were suggestions that around 30 had left globally, including for private equity firms and rival banks. Deutsche declined to comment at the time.

item.title: Financial services hiring is looking up, if you look at it right
item.description:
Is financial services hiring increasing towards the end of the year? Are financial services firms cutting back their junior hiring due to AI? Are hedge funds hiring? These are complicated questions, and they are the sort of questions that you can ask in an AMA on our forum for financial services professionals, the bubble <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/t/recruiter-ama-financial-services-michael-page/6301/10>.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/signup>✍️
Jonny Gilmore has been a recruiter with Michael Page - our ideal recruiter in financial services </ideal-recruiter> - for two decades. It’s a long time – long enough to see a few crashes, and a few meteoric rises. Gilmore thinks we’re on the cusp of a less meteoric rise now – more of “a slight upward trajectory.”
Gilmore cites UK Office for National Statistics data saying that there were around 34,000 jobs open in UK financial services in the first half of 2024, and around 32,000 in the first half of 2026, which he called "a flat line," noting that the Q3 figures were only a "marginal" slowdown. Gilmore thinks there’s every reason to be optimistic about Q4.
The impact of AI on hiring, therefore, might be overblown. “A number of the major banks that I talk to,” Gilmore says, are committing “to their graduate hiring programmes, and the reason for that is because it’s the right thing to do ethically.”
Gilmore did not disclose his clients, but it’s not a surprise that these commitments are happening. The UK government has asked finance firms to pledge <https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a4f76e72467584757371b36/Financial_Services_Skills_Compact.pdf> that they will “maintain and/or grow structured routes into our organisation for new talent.”
It’s interesting that banks would need to pledge to do something they want to do for ethical reasons. Revelio Labs <https://www.reveliolabs.com/news/ai-and-work/ai-junior-bankers-hiring-data>, a market intelligence firm, found that junior roles at US banks have decreased in the last four years (since the introduction of GPT-3.5, basically) while senior roles have increased. “The industry is restructuring around AI rather than being automated by it,” Revelio said.
The strongest demand that Gilmore sees is in fintech and data roles, where vacancies have increased by 50%, he says. At the banks and investment managers that Gilmore recruits for, vacancies are up 15% year on year, mostly in operations, regulatory roles, and transformation. Risk, compliance and regulatory reporting are "just resilient", he says.
Some hedge funds and investment managers "have been doing things really well, but in the same way for 20 or 30 years", Gilmore says, and are now hiring to modernise their technology stacks. But hedge fund hiring in general is slowing. Goldman Sachs’s research <https://hedgeweek.com/news/hedge-fund-hiring-slows-as-multistrategy-firms-expand-external-allocations> this month showed headcount at multi-strategy </news/goldman-sachs-md-says-multistrategy-hedge-funds-may-yet-need-many-more-p-ms> funds grew 7% in the year to mid-2026, down from 27% in 2023, with less hiring outside investment roles.
Jonny Gilmore is answering questions on the bubble, our forum for financial services professionals today. Sign up and ask a question today! <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/t/recruiter-ama-financial-services-michael-page/6301/10>

item.title: The Italian stallion rides again in Barclays' rates business
item.description:
As we reported last week, Barclays' macro business has lost Hamza Houmaddy </news/barclays-s-head-of-european-rates-trading-is-leaving>, its popular European head of rates trading. This seems unfortunate, but is maybe fine because an old face has simultaneously reappeared.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Julien Ercole, an Italian trader who insiders say is known for huge and successful risk-taking and who disappeared to hedge fund </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job> Point72 in late 2023, has returned. Barclays declined to comment and Ercole didn't respond to a request to comment but the FCA Register shows him arriving at the bank on October 5th.
Ercole is not thought to be directly replacing Houmaddy, but insiders say he has a reputation for being ambitious and may want a big job. Last time he was at Barclays, he was head of peripheral government bond trading, based in Milan. He's understood to have made his name trading CCTs, or Italian floating rate bonds and to have conjured a nine figure profit from this before he left.
Ercole spent 17 months at Point72 and left in March 2025. He's returned to Barclays at an interesting time following the departure of Houmaddy and poor performance of the European rates business, which was called out in Barclays' Q3 results. </news/barclays-fixed-income-traders-are-getting-bigger-bonuses-at-just-the-wrong-time>It presumably didn't help that Barclays has been diverting money away from its macro business and towards prime services as it intentionally rebalances <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-24/barclays-house-of-fixed-income-pins-future-growth-on-equities?utm_medium=email&utm_source=author_alert&utm_term=261024&utm_campaign=author_21061455> in favour of equities.
Barclays' rates business includes some remarkable specimens. Mark Wade </news/barclays-hired-the-whale-from-nomura> from Nomura joined as a trader earlier this month. Puni Raja </news/punitha-raja-barclays> in sales is thought to be having a big year.
Ercole has good credentials. Like many Italians in the market he studied at Bocconi. Then he completed a Master's </news/the-top-30-masters-in-finance-for-getting-a-job-in-investment-banking>at the LSE.

item.title: Morning Coffee: Hedge fund recruiter on $800k is unhappy in Hong Kong. Goldman Sachs' rehired partner was a good buy
item.description:
How much do you earn as a senior business development professional who recruits portfolio managers (PM) for a hedge fund? Based upon a recently filed court document in Hong Kong, you won't get as much as an actual PM, but you will still get a lot.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Reporting on the filing, Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-27/hedge-fund-verition-sued-by-ex-asia-business-development-head?taid=6ae02fe408444f00015c8429&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>notes that Elizabeth Xiang spent nearly five years working for Verition, the friendlyish multistrategy hedge fund. Xiang was Asia-Pacific head of business development there and her court filing says Verition’s headcount in the region grew from four to 87 during her time. Thirty PMs were hired locally and Xiang says she was responsible for 27 of them.
As a reward for her efforts, Xiang says she was paid a salary of around US$200k in 2025, plus a bonus of roughly $600k. When she joined in 2021, her salary was $150k, and she says her bonus rose every year. Times were good.
In late 2025, though, Xiang's mother in China had a cancer relapse and she spent early 2026 travelling to and fro to care for her. Xiang says Verition started a new project to map portfolio managers in the APAC market without telling her. Then she says the fund suddenly fired her in June, citing “failure to consistently follow reasonable management instructions,” “inconsistent follow-through” and “ongoing communication concerns with internal and external stakeholders.” Xiang claims she was fired because she took time off to care for her mother and because Verition didn't want to pay her 2026 bonus.
Verition didn't comment for Bloomberg's article. We have contacted the fund for comment. The account of Xiang's employment and firing is therefore drawn from her own perspective. Bloomberg says she plans to file for discrimination too. Working as a bus dev in hedge funds is good, until it's not.
Separately, it's not really so long ago that Nick Giovanni </news/goldman-sachs-partner-retired-return>galloped back to Goldman Sachs after an eight month holiday and three and a half years at Instacart, during which the company completed a $660m IPO and Giovanni presumably became quite rich.
A lesser man might have retired at this point but as we noted in February, Giovanni is very passionate about being a banker and has said things like: “Advising founders, executives and boards is what I love to do."
This is fortunate for Goldman Sachs, because yesterday the bank won yet another prestigious lead left position on a key 2026 IPO, this time Anthropic's. Giovanni and Jung Min - a Goldman TMT banker friendly with NVIDIA - appear to be the Goldman bankers responsible for this.
Giovanni's passion is less fortunate for Morgan Stanley, which has once again </news/space-x-ipo-goldman-sachs-morgan-stanley> been relegated to the position of stabilisation agent. This is contrary to earlier reports </news/anthropic-ipo-morgan-stanley-goldman-sachs> that Morgan Stanley was going to be lead left this time after sadly ceding the position to Goldman on the SpaceX IPO. It may also be contrary to Morgan Stanley's own expectations. Bloomberg <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/goldman-s-210-billion-day-of-deals-driven-by-ai-financing-fever>notes that Morgan Stanley led Anthropic's $15bn revolving credit line. Its bankers may have expected to get prime position on the IPO as a result. It was not to be; Giovanni is too passionate.
Meanwhile...
Anthropic has seven co-founders. They will each be worth more than $13bn. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/anthropic-s-seven-founders-are-worth-more-than-13-billion-each?taid=6adf97821579270001ce0d28&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Revenue per employee at Anthropic is over $6.6 million as of September 30, 2026, compared to $1.4 million as of September 30, 2025. (Anthropic prospectus, marked up) <https://docs.pe.finance/anthropic-s1/>
Citadel Securities is getting a bigger India office. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/ken-griffin-s-citadel-securities-to-expand-india-office>
Balyasny hired Matti Konsala from Citi for equities algo trading. (Trade) <https://www.thetradenews.com/balyasny-am-adds-citi-equities-algo-trader-to-systematic-trading-team/>
Capula is opening an Athens office and wants someone to set it up. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/capula-explores-greek-office-in-move-following-rokos-millennium?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter>
AI could do the work of credit traders. Credit investors and traders are already asking Agentic BondGPT to alert them when a CCC bond trades more than 50 basis points wide from its prior day close. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/ai-agents-seen-taking-credit-trading-work-from-humans-over-time?srnd=phx-markets>
Microsoft is offering 60,000 employees a great chance to become unemployed. “This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support.” Standard severance will be paid. (Bloomberg) <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/microsoft-to-offer-buyouts-to-60-000-workers-in-latest-cost-cut?taid=6adf907bd939c80001a7c6d3&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_content=business&utm_medium=social&utm_source=twitter>
Ondřej Surý fixed the PHP flaws without being paid. He did get $10k in donations. (BBC) <https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw30ejqljl43o>
No one is leaving Deloitte either. The voluntary attrition rate there for the 2025/26 financial year was 10.3%, according to the pay report. That’s slightly up from 10% in 2025 and 9.4% in 2024, but below its pre-pandemic level of 12.8% in 2020 and 14.8% in 2019. (Financial News) <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/deloittes-uk-pay-report-shines-spotlight-on-attrition-ceo-pay-and-diversity-d408653e>
The tragic tale of the man who exposed Howard Lutnick's links to Jeffrey Epstein. “I’ve lost all my money, my wife and I are separated, and I’m in danger of having my home repossessed. Speaking out has devastated my life.” Two months later he was dead. The FCA is accused of failing to protect him. (Banker) <https://www.thebanker.com/content/f16e27fb-e461-4853-8128-f088ff00dc29>

item.title: HSBC may increase bonuses. Hong Kong bankers may get them
item.description:
HSBC results are out. After what the bank describes as a “strong” third quarter in which profits across the bank rose 32% as a more “simplified and agile” HSBC emerged, HSBC is considering increasing bonuses. Based upon Q3 results, lucky bankers and traders may receive them.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Revenues in HSBC’s Hong Kong corporate and institutional bank (CIB) rose 24% year-on-year in the third quarter, versus a paltry 6% increase in the non-ring fenced bank in the UK where the London bankers and traders sit. Revenues in the Middle East, excluding Saudi Arabia, fell 2%. Profits in the Hong Kong CIB were up 70%, versus a drop of 5% in the UK once unusually high costs relating to last year’s restructuring are removed.
HSBC has indicated that it will be paying bonuses </news/hsbc-bonuses-2026> proportionate to performance now that it's liberated from the EU bonus cap. Last year, the average bonus for its material risk takers was $819k. This year, CFO Pam Kaur said the bank is considering increasing variable pay (bonuses) if strong performance continues. Pre-tax profit in the CIB is up 16% year-on-year across the first nine months as a whole.
Kaur said that the bank's surprise decision </news/hscb-closure-europe-us-job-cuts>to simplify itself by pulling out of M&A and ECM in Europe and the US and to focus on the Middle East and Asia is going well. <https://www.fnlondon.com/articles/hsbc-cfo-says-dealmaking-pivot-to-asia-and-middle-east-has-paid-off-dfbacbda?mod=homepage>“We are working around on around 70 live IPO mandates, of which more than 40 are in Hong Kong, and with over 25, we have a sponsor role,” she declared.
HSBC doesn’t break out performance in fixed income and equities sales and trading, or the performance of M&A, ECM or DCM bankers. Excluding FX trading, which has been shunted into wholesale transaction banking, sales and trading revenues at HSBC were up an impressive 69% in Q3. Investment banking revenues rose by a less impressive 12%, what with European and US banking closures last year.
Kaur said HSBC won't make a final decision on higher bonuses until January. When she does, who will get them? Maybe FX traders, whom Kaur says have been thriving in the transaction bank, where FX revenues rose 19% in Q3. Maybe Hong Kong bankers with all their mandates. Maybe Hong Kong traders. Maybe people in financing and prime broking, whom HSBC said are thriving with "increased volumes and wider margins”. Maybe even bankers and traders in London and the US. On a nine month basis, profit growth at the US CIB has outperformed the other regions and the Middle East and Asia don't look quite so impressive.
Last year, there was some whinging from HSBC employees about the allocation of bonuses in London. There were also job cuts a few weeks before bonuses were announced. HSBC's London bankers and traders also like to complain that costs are disproportionately allocated to their entity.
HSBC hasn’t finished cost cutting. It still plans to cut $100m of costs in the fourth quarter. Once that's done, it will have finally achieved its $2bn annualised target. Hooray.

item.title: "Hedge funds hired too many morons" and other unpopular opinions as the industry pukes PMs
item.description:
Spare a thought for the hedge funds </news/how-to-get-a-hedge-fund-job>. As we reported last week, both macro </news/london-s-macro-hedge-fund-pain-as-up-to-100-people-are-out-everyone-has-blown-up>and credit funds </news/european-high-yield> have been flooding the street with newly unwanted talent. Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage </news/prime-broking-banks-2026> desk said <https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-23/hedge-funds-log-widest-daily-drawdown-since-covid-in-stock-rout> last week that funds have also experienced one of their broadest equities declines since the COVID pandemic. All is pain.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
Portfolio managers </news/finance/portfolio-manager-job-hedge-fund-lifestyle> are suffering. A chart has been circulating on X <https://x.com/AndreasSteno/status/2113651945122443273?s=20>suggesting 100 PMs are out so far this month, versus 40 in September and closer to 20 before that. Hedge fund headhunters say the number of people out of the market is enormous.
The reasons for the PM exits vary by strategy, but most were stopped out after making losses that exceed their risk limits. In credit, there are issues with weak covenants, regulatory intervention and rising rates. </news/european-high-yield>In macro, leveraged trades on French government bonds blew up. </news/european-high-yield>In equities, tech stocks sold off. Even multistrategy funds, supposedly insulated against issues from individual strategies were down 1.9% on Thursday according to Goldman data.
Not everyone is sympathetic. As hedge funds have increased their assets under management, headcount at leading funds has increased substantially </news/multistrategy-hedge-funds-hiring>with many new hires drawn from banks. ADV forms indicate that 2,000 people were added last year alone. Some in the industry say funds have been scraping the barrel.
"Hedge funds hired too many morons," says one US portfolio manager. "A lot of people in funds are now very unimpressive," he adds. "There are a lot of clowns who were just long bonds and who have been killed."
Instead of PMs in funds originating trade ideas, he says the model has reversed. "The sellside pitches the ideas and people start to get in on a trade. Then other banks keep repeating the same ideas, and so buyside people keep getting in the same trade until it’s too crowded."
It ends in a situation where the majority of the buyside is on a similar trade until something happens to reverse it, he says. "And then they can’t get out fast enough because they don’t have enough understanding of the fundamentals and factors that causing problems to that trade."
As funds have scrambled to increase headcount, he says they've hired too many juniors from banks. But banks themselves already lost their best senior traders to hedge funds years ago and the juniors being hired have lacked guidance from talented traders. "There are no mentors left on the sellside to coach juniors," says another portfolio manager.
Coupled with the fact that the job of a portfolio manager is very different to the job of a trader on a desk in a bank, this has contributed to the blow-ups, say observers. "It is a very different world being a market making junior on a desk to trying to trade against the spread. You are not just doing trades and hedging against a book but are exposed to market moves and the dislocations that have happened this year," says one industry insider.
All of this implies that portfolio managers leaving now will find it hard to get new roles. Many are on non-competes anyway. Some have only recently been hired and are on guarantees.
Some in the market strongly disagree with the framing above, though. One young PM tells us the losses and stopping-outs have nothing to do with PM ability and everything to do with the growing size of funds. Freddie Parks, head of Goldman Sachs' prime broking team, said in September that $500bn had flowed into multistrategy funds in the previous 12 months. </news/goldman-sachs-md-says-multistrategy-hedge-funds-may-yet-need-many-more-p-ms>
"The real cause is that hedge fund AUM have exploded, so everything is more crowded and markets can’t absorb that much liquidity," says the young PM. It's not the fault of the young traders hired from banks. If anything, he says they are very risk averse because they weren't taught about real risk-taking in banks. Some funds charge PMs for the capital allocated to them, creating pressure to put capital to work even in difficult markets.
At some point, funds will need to hire new people. There are rumours of non-competes being shortened to facilitate this. Some of those now out of the market will have to come back in a different guise, says Richard Averill at Waterline Compensation, <https://waterlineeconomics.com/> which models hedge fund pay. "Most teams have a strategy that differentiates them from other PMs, but if your strategy no longer works, you don’t just have bad positions, you have a strategy that no longer makes sense."

item.title: Citi has picked up yet another Deutsche Bank MD. In LevFin, this time
item.description:
Some of the most iconic combinations in history need no introduction. Laurel and Hardy in America, Fry and Laurie in the UK. Enemies to lovers on Ao3. In finance, it seems to increasingly be “joined Citi” and “left Deutsche Bank”.
Click here to join the bubble by eFinancialCareers, our new anonymous community. <https://bubble.efinancialcareers.com/login?_gl=1*ut8n6u*_gcl_au*MTg4MDY2NTExNi4xNzYxNTU3NDIz*_ga*ODczNzI2NTA0LjE3NTM2OTk2ODI.*_ga_NZFQV4MXPM*czE3NjM2NDM0MDYkbzI1NiRnMSR0MTc2MzY0MzQzOSRqMjckbDAkaDMyMjc4OTUzMw..>✍️
Ilir Hasi joined Citi in New York this month as a managing director </news/banks-weird-hierarchies-analysts-associates-vps-mds> (MD) in its Leveraged Finance (LevFin) team. He joined Citi from Deutsche Bank in the city, where he spent seven and a half years, and was made an MD in 2024 </news/deutsche-bank-s-new-managing-directors>. Hasi was at BMO Capital Markets before that. Citi did not respond to a request for comment.
LevFin has seen better days. US Treasury yields hit multi-decade highs in September, and equity and debt issuance slowed late in the third quarter. In July, asset management firm PIMCO warned <https://www.pimco.com/gb/en/insights/the-credit-market-lens-a-growing-divide-in-leveraged-finance> that distress is likely to rise in leveraged loans, even if the economy holds up, blaming the private credit fundraising boom (and the subsequent struggles of software companies in the AI world. High yield has suffered </news/european-high-yield> in particular.
Nonetheless, Citi has stacked up on LevFin talent, including from Deutsche Bank – Ludovic Ingelaere joined Citi from Deutsche in Paris as an MD in its LevFin team in July last year. It also hired Jenner Kizer </news/citi-hired-a-lev-fin-guy-from-deutsche-bank-and-he-is-moving-on> from Deutsche back in 2022. Citi has hired a lot of people </news/citi-hiring-deutsche-bank> from Deutsche Bank in general, recently - Citi's banking head, Vis Raghavan, said <https://www.wsj.com/finance/banking/the-outsider-trying-to-restore-citi-to-investment-banking-glory-b2802e99?st=z6UoP4&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink> back in 2024 about wanting to invest in the bank's financial sponsors team. Expanding his bank's LevFin abilities is part of that. The firm has hired sponsors bankers substantially, including recently - Antonio Iannella joined the firm as a sponsors MD in Milan earlier this month, for example.
LevFin can pay very well when the times are good. A compensation report from earlier this year from Prospect Rock Partners found that </news/the-best-leveraged-finance-m-ds-earn-the-most-now-directors-not-so-much> LevFin MDs earned $1.6m on average for their work in 2025, much higher than the rest of their investment banking peers, who earned an average of $1.1m in the same period. 2026 might be even better; Citi’s Q3 results a few weeks ago noted that a decline in debt capital markets </news/capital-markets-jobs-ecm-and-dcm> revenue was “primarily” offset by a growth in leveraged finance revenue.

item.title: What to expect from the case study in a private credit interview
item.description:
If you want to work in a private credit </news/private-credit>fund in London, you may have encountered Richard Hoar.
Hoar is a director at recruitment firm Goodman Masson, who specialises in private credit </news/how-to-get-a-job-in-private-equity> jobs. He cut his teeth recruiting for middle and back office jobs in the early 2000s, but has “moved up the value chain.” So has the recruitment market, says Hoar.
💥Follow us on WhatsApp for news alerts. <https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VacsPmzKGGGK91C7dR39>💥
For all the bad press about redemptions from private credit funds and fraud-induced losses at the likes of Jefferies and Barclays, Hoar says private credit jobs retain their appeal. “It’s the buyside,” he explains. “You’re the principal, that’s more glamorous.”
While private equity funds provide capital that gives them a share in the equity of companies that are not publicly traded on exchanges, private credit funds make loans to companies that either can’t or don’t want to borrow in other ways. Private equity firms like to hire former M&A </news/get-a-job-in-ma> juniors; private credit firms like to hire former leveraged finance bankers.
Hoar says competition for places in private credit firms remains intense. “The funnel is sharp,” he says. Hundreds of people are filtered out after sending in CVs. 20-25 might get through to the first interview. 12 might get through to the second round interview. Six get through to the case study. Two get offers.
If you make it through to the case study, you are therefore doing well. Hoar says the case studies typically involve a presentation based around company accounts.
“You will have 3-4 hours to prepare the presentation and they will often put mistakes in there that they you want you to spot,” he says. The emphasis is on identifying errors in covenants and documentation that might make the deal too friendly towards the borrower, plus reasons why the fund might make a loss. You’ll be asked to produce a memorandum on the deal and will be interrogated on this, says Hoar.
How can you prepare? Make sure you’re familiar with covenants and loan documentation. Make sure you can read a balance sheet.
Make sure, too, that you are used to presenting and to defending your case. “They want to see that you have attention to detail, can tell a story and can handle yourself under pressure,” says Hoar. “There will often be a good cop- bad cop approach to see if you can still handle yourself and come up with the right answers when you’re under pressure.”
